author: richard-sibbes
fields.title: The Bruised Reed
fields.subtitle: And Smoking Flax
fields.description: Isaiah promised that the bruised reed would not be broken and the smoking flax not quenched, and Sibbes spends this book on what that means for people who feel they are barely alight. It is the gentlest of the Puritan classics, written for the discouraged, the half-converted and the spiritually exhausted, and unwilling at any point to press harder on someone already bent. Richard Baxter read it and was changed by it; so have generations who found that nothing else in that century would let them be weak.
fields.about_html:
Sibbes takes a single line from Isaiah, quoted by Matthew about Christ — “a bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench” — and writes an entire book to people who are afraid they are too far gone. His argument is that the bruising is not evidence against them, and that a faith which is all smoke and no flame is still fire.

Sibbes preached in London in the 1620s, to a generation raised on a searching kind of self-examination that could tip over into despair — believers taught to look for evidence of grace in themselves and finding little. This is the pastoral correction to that, from inside the same tradition: not less seriousness about sin, but a different place to look for assurance.

Both halves of the image matter to him. A bruised reed is not a broken one, and smoking flax is a wick that has gone out but still has fire in it: what looks like failure is, in his reading, the thing being kept alight. He is careful not to make this cheap — he has a great deal to say about not mistaking sloth for weakness — but the direction of the whole book is that Christ does not finish off what is already damaged.

Richard Baxter read it at fifteen and said it made the difference: “Sibbes opened more the love of God to me, and gave me a livelier apprehension of the mystery of redemption and how much I was beholden to Jesus Christ.” It has done the same for readers in that condition ever since, and it is short.

fields.title: The Text Opened and Divided: What the Reed Is, and What the Bruising Is
fields.body_html:
THE prophet Isaiah, lifted up and carried on the wing of the prophetic spirit, passes over all the time between himself and the appearing of Jesus Christ in the flesh. With the eye of prophecy and the eye of faith he sees Christ as present, and in God’s name he presents Him to the spiritual eye of others in these words: Behold my servant whom I have chosen, etc. Saint Matthew quotes this passage as now fulfilled in Christ. In it we are shown, first, the calling of Christ to His office.

Secondly, how He carries it out.

As for His calling: God calls Him here His righteous servant, etc. Christ was God’s servant in the greatest piece of service there ever was, a chosen and choice servant. He did and suffered everything by commission from the Father. In this we may see God’s sweet love to us: He counts the work of our salvation by Christ His greatest service, and He is willing to put His only beloved Son to that service. He may well put [Behold] in front of it, to raise our thoughts to the highest pitch of attention and wonder. In times of temptation, troubled consciences look so hard at their present trouble that they need to be roused to behold Him in whom they may find rest for their distressed souls. In temptations it is safest to look at nothing but Christ, the true bronze serpent, the true Lamb of God that taketh away the sins of the world (John 1:29). This saving sight brings a special comfort into the soul, especially if we look not only at Christ but at the Father’s authority and love in Him. For in everything Christ did and suffered as Mediator, we must see God in Him reconciling the world to Himself (2 Corinthians 5:19).

What a support this is to our faith, that God the Father, the one offended by our sins, is so well pleased with the work of redemption! And what a comfort it is that, since God’s love rests on Christ and He is well pleased in Him, we may conclude that He is just as well pleased with us if we are in Christ! For His love rests on the whole Christ, on Christ mystical (His body, the Church) as well as Christ natural, because He loves Him and us with one love. So let us embrace Christ, and God’s love in Him, and build our faith safely on a Saviour who comes with so high a commission.

See here, for our comfort, the sweet agreement of all three persons. The Father gives Christ a commission; the Spirit equips Him and sets Him apart for it; Christ Himself carries out the office of Mediator. Our redemption is founded on the joint agreement of all three persons of the Trinity.

As for how He carries out His calling, it is described here as modest, without making a noise or raising dust by any grand arrival, as princes usually do: [his voice shall not be heard]. His voice was indeed heard, but what voice? Come unto me, all ye that are weary and heavy laden (Matthew 11:28). He cried out, but how? Ho, every one that thirsteth, come, etc. (Isaiah 55:1). And just as His coming was modest, it was also gentle, as these words show: The bruised reed shall he not break. In these words we may observe three things. First, the condition of those Christ had to deal with: 1. They were bruised reeds. 2. They were smoking flax. Secondly, how Christ behaves toward them: He did not break the bruised reed or quench the smoking flax. More is meant here than is said, for He will not only not break the bruised reed or quench the flax, but will cherish them.

Thirdly, the constancy and progress of this tender care of His, until judgment come to victory: that is, until the holy work of grace begun in their hearts is brought to such perfection that it wins out over all the corruption that opposes it.

First, then, the condition of the people He was to deal with is that they were bruised reeds and smoking flax: not trees but reeds, and not whole reeds but bruised ones. The Church is compared to weak things: to a dove among the birds, to a vine among the plants, to sheep among the animals, to a woman, who is the weaker vessel. And here God’s children are compared to bruised reeds and smoking flax. We will speak of them first as bruised reeds, and then as smoking flax. They are bruised reeds before their conversion, and often after it. Before conversion all of them are, except those raised in the Church to whom God has delighted to show Himself gracious from childhood; yet they are bruised in different degrees, as God sees fit. The difference depends on temperament, gifts, way of life and so on, and also on how God means to use them in time to come; for usually He empties people of themselves and makes them nothing before He will use them in any great service.

This bruised reed is a person who is usually in some misery, as those were who came to Christ for help, and who is brought by his misery to see that sin is its cause. For whatever excuses sin makes, its end is bruising or breaking. He feels his sin and misery to the point of being bruised by them. Seeing no help in himself, he is carried along by a restless desire to be supplied by someone else, with some hope that raises him a little out of himself toward Christ, though he does not yet dare to claim any share in mercy. This spark of hope, opposed by doubts and fears that rise from corruption, makes him like smoking flax. So the two together, a bruised reed and smoking flax, make up the state of a poor distressed person. He is what our Saviour Christ calls poor in spirit (Matthew 5:3): one who sees his lack, and also sees that he is in debt to Divine Justice, with no way of paying it from himself or any creature. So he mourns, and on some hope of mercy from the promise, and from the examples of those who have obtained mercy, he is stirred up to hunger and thirst for it.

fields.title: Those Christ Deals With Are Bruised
fields.body_html:
THIS bruising is needed before conversion, so that the Spirit may make a way for Himself into the heart by levelling all proud, lofty thoughts, and so that we may understand ourselves to be what we really are by nature. We love to wander from ourselves and be strangers at home, until God bruises us by one cross or another. Then we come to our senses and come home to ourselves, like the prodigal (Luke 15:17). It is an extraordinarily hard thing to bring a dull and evasive heart to cry for mercy with real feeling. Like criminals, our hearts never cry for the Judge’s mercy until they have been beaten out of every excuse. Again, this bruising makes us set a high value on Christ. Then the gospel is truly the gospel; then the fig leaves of morality will do us no good. It makes us more thankful, and through thankfulness more fruitful in our lives. For what makes so many people so cold and barren, except that no bruising for sin ever made God’s grace dear to them? This dealing of God also settles us more firmly in His ways, after we have had knocks and bruises in our own ways. This is often the cause of relapses and falling away: people never smarted for sin at the beginning; they were not long enough under the lash of the law. So this lower work of the Spirit, bringing down lofty thoughts, is necessary before conversion. And usually, to further the work of conviction, the Holy Spirit adds some affliction, which, when made holy, has a healing and cleansing power.

In fact, we need bruising even after conversion. Reeds need it so that they know they are reeds and not oaks. Even reeds need bruising, because of the pride still left in our nature, and to let us see that we live by mercy. It also keeps weaker Christians from being too discouraged when they see stronger ones shaken and bruised. So Peter was bruised when he wept bitterly. Until he met with this bruise, this reed had more wind in him than substance: Though all forsake thee, I will not, etc. (Matthew 26:35). God’s people cannot do without these examples. The heroic deeds of those great worthies do not comfort the church as much as their falls and bruises do (Psalm 32:3–5). So David was bruised until he came to a free confession, without deceit in his spirit; indeed, his sorrows rose in his own feeling to the exquisite pain of broken bones (Psalm 51:8). So Hezekiah complains that God had broken his bones like a lion (Isaiah 38:13). So that chosen vessel, St. Paul, needed the messenger of Satan to buffet him, so that he would not be lifted up beyond measure (2 Corinthians 12:7).

From this we learn that we must not judge ourselves or others too harshly when God puts us through bruise after bruise. We must be conformed to Christ our head, who was bruised for us (Isaiah 53:5), so that we may know how much we owe Him. Worldly spirits, ignorant of God’s ways of bringing His children to heaven, condemn broken-hearted Christians as hopeless cases, when in fact God is doing a gracious, good work in them. It is no easy matter to bring someone from nature to grace and from grace to glory, so unyielding and unmanageable are our hearts.

fields.title: Christ Will Not Break the Bruised Reed
fields.body_html:
THE second point is that Christ will not break the bruised reed. Doctors may put their patients through a great deal of pain, but they will not destroy the body’s strength; they build it up step by step. Surgeons will lance and cut, but they will not dismember. A mother with a sick and fretful child will not throw it away because of that. And shall there be more mercy in the stream than in the spring? Shall we think there is more mercy in ourselves than in God, who plants the feeling of mercy in us? To show Christ’s mercy to all bruised reeds more fully, consider the comforting relationships He has taken on: husband, shepherd, brother and so on. He will fulfil them to the utmost. For shall others, by His grace, fulfil what He calls them to, and not He who out of His love has taken on these relationships, so firmly grounded on His Father’s appointment and His own free undertaking? Consider the names He borrows from the gentlest creatures, such as lamb and hen, to show His tender care. Consider His very name, Jesus, a Saviour, given Him by God Himself. Consider His office, which matches His name: He was to heal the broken-hearted (Isaiah 61:1). At His baptism the Holy Spirit rested on Him in the form of a dove, to show that He would be a gentle, dove-like Mediator. See how graciously He carries out His offices. As a prophet, He came with blessing in His mouth: Blessed be the poor in spirit, etc. (Matthew 5). He invited those to come to Him whose hearts raised the most objections against themselves: Come unto me, all ye that are weary and heavy laden (Matthew 11:28). How His heart was moved when He saw the people as sheep without a shepherd (Matthew 9:36)! He never turned anyone back who came to Him, though some went away of their own accord. He came as a priest to die for His enemies. In the days of His flesh He gave His disciples a form of prayer, putting requests to God into their mouths and His Spirit to intercede in their hearts; and now He intercedes in heaven for weak Christians, standing between God’s anger and them. He shed tears for those who shed His blood. So He is a gentle king. He will let mourners into His presence; He is a king of the poor and afflicted. As He has beams of majesty, so He has a heart of mercy and compassion; He is the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6). Why was He tempted, except so that He might help those who are tempted (Hebrews 2:18)? What mercy may we not expect from so gracious a Mediator (1 Timothy 2:5), who took our nature on Himself so that He might be gracious? He is a doctor skilled with every disease, especially at binding up a broken heart. He died so that He might heal our souls with a plaster of His own blood, and by that death save us from the death we had brought on ourselves by our own sins. And does He not have the same heart in heaven? Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me? (Acts 9:4), cried the head in heaven when the foot was trodden on earth. His exaltation has not made Him forget His own flesh. Though it has freed Him from suffering, it has not freed Him from compassion toward us. The Lion of the tribe of Judah will tear in pieces only those who will not have Him rule over them (Luke 19:27). He will not show His strength against those who throw themselves down before Him.

What should we learn from this, but to come boldly to the throne of grace with all our troubles? Shall our sins discourage us, when He appears there only for sinners? Are you bruised? Take heart; He is calling you. Do not hide your wounds; lay everything open before Him; do not keep Satan’s secrets. Go to Christ, even trembling. Like the poor woman, if we can only touch the hem of His garment (Matthew 9:20), we will be healed and receive a gracious answer. Go boldly to God in our flesh; it is so that we might go boldly to Him that He is flesh of our flesh and bone of our bone. Never be afraid to go to God, since we have such a Mediator with Him, who is not only our friend but our brother and husband. Well might the angels proclaim from heaven, Behold, we bring you tidings of joy (Luke 2:10). Well might the apostle stir us up to rejoice in the Lord again and again (Philippians 4:4); he knew very well what grounds he had for it. Peace and joy are two main fruits of His kingdom. Let the world be as it will; if we cannot rejoice in the world, we can still rejoice in the Lord. His presence makes any condition comfortable. Be not afraid, He says to His disciples when they were afraid as if they had seen a ghost, it is I (Matthew 14:27); as if there were no cause for fear where He is present.

Let this steady us when we feel ourselves bruised. Christ’s way is first to wound and then to heal. No sound, whole soul will ever enter heaven. In temptation, think: Christ was tempted for me; my graces and comforts will match my trials. If Christ is so merciful that He will not break me, I will not break myself by despair, nor hand myself over to that roaring lion, Satan, to break me to pieces.

Thirdly, see how opposite Christ’s disposition is to that of Satan and his agents. Satan attacks us when we are weakest, as Simeon and Levi attacked the Shechemites when they were sore (Genesis 34:25). But Christ will repair in us all the breaches sin and Satan have made; He binds up the broken-hearted. And as a mother takes most tender care of the sickest and weakest child, so Christ inclines most mercifully toward the weakest. He also puts an instinct into the weakest things to lean on something stronger than themselves for support. The vine props itself on the elm, and the weakest creatures often have the strongest shelters. The Church’s awareness of her weakness makes her willing to lean on her Beloved and hide herself under His wing.

fields.title: Signs of One Truly Bruised; the Means and Measure of Bruising; Comfort for Such
fields.body_html:
BUT how can we know whether we are among those who may expect mercy?

By bruising here is not meant those who are brought low only by hardships, but those who are brought by them to see their sin, which bruises most of all. When the conscience is under the guilt of sin, every judgment brings the soul news of God’s anger, and all lesser troubles flow into this great trouble of conscience over sin. Just as all bad humours run to the diseased and bruised part of the body, and every creditor descends on the debtor once he is arrested, so when the conscience is once awakened, all past sins and present hardships join together to make the bruise more painful. Now whoever is bruised like this will be satisfied with nothing but mercy from the One who bruised him. He has wounded, and He must heal: Lord, You have bruised me as I deserved for my sins; bind up my heart again, etc. 2. Again, a person who is truly bruised judges sin to be the greatest evil and God’s favour the greatest good. 3. He would rather hear of mercy than of a kingdom. 4. He has a low opinion of himself and thinks he is not worth the ground he walks on. 5. He is not quick to judge others, being taken up with his own heart, but is full of sympathy and compassion for those under God’s hand. 6. He thinks those who walk in the comforts of God’s Spirit are the happiest people in the world. 7. He trembles at the word of God (Isaiah 66:2), and honours the very feet of those blessed messengers who bring him peace (Romans 10:15). 8. He is more taken up with the inward exercises of a broken heart than with outward form, yet he is careful to use all the holy means through which comfort comes.

But how can we come to have this frame of mind?

First, we must think of bruising either as a state God brings us into or as a duty we are to carry out. Both are meant here. We must join with God in bruising ourselves. When He humbles us, let us humble ourselves and not hold out against Him, or He will double His blows. And let us acknowledge that Christ is right in all His chastening, knowing that all His dealings with us are meant to make us turn back into our own hearts. His work in bruising us aims at our work of bruising ourselves. Let us grieve over our own stubbornness and say, Lord, what a heart I have, that needs all this, that none of it could be spared! We must lay siege to the hardness of our own hearts and weigh up our sin as heavily as we can. We must look on Christ, who was bruised for us, and look on Him whom we have pierced with our sins. But no directions will succeed unless God, by His Spirit, convicts us deeply, setting our sins before us and bringing us to a standstill. Then we will set out for mercy. Conviction will produce contrition, and contrition will produce humility. So ask God to bring a clear, strong light into every corner of our souls, and to send with it a spirit of power to lay our hearts low.

No fixed amount of bruising ourselves can be prescribed. But it must go so far that, 1. we value Christ above everything and see that we must have a Saviour; and 2. that we correct whatever is wrong, even if it means cutting off our right hand or plucking out our right eye. There is a dangerous making light of the work of humbling. Some use the fact that Christ will not break the bruised reed as an excuse for dealing superficially with their own hearts. But such people must understand that not every sudden fright or brief sorrow makes us bruised reeds. It is not just hanging our heads for a while like a bulrush (Isaiah 58:5). It is working our hearts into such sorrow that sin becomes more hateful to us than punishment, until we do holy violence against it. Otherwise, by going easy on ourselves, we make work for God to bruise us and for bitter repentance later. I admit it is dangerous in some cases, with some temperaments, to press this bruising too hard and too long, because they may die under the wound and the burden before they are raised up again. So in mixed congregations it is good to mix in comfort, so that every soul may have its proper portion. But if we lay this down as a foundation, that there is more mercy in Christ than sin in us, there can be no danger in dealing thoroughly. It is better to go to heaven bruised than to hell sound. So let us not let ourselves off too soon, or pull off the plaster before the cure is done, but keep ourselves under this work until sin is the bitterest of all things and Christ the sweetest. And whenever God’s hand is on us in any way, it is good to turn our sorrow over other things toward the root of them all, which is sin. Let our grief run mostly in that channel, so that just as sin produced grief, grief may consume sin.

But are we not bruised unless we grieve more for sin than for punishment?

Sometimes the grief from outward troubles may weigh more heavily on the soul than grief for God’s displeasure. In such cases the grief works on the whole person, outward and inward, and has nothing to hold it back except a small spark of faith, whose working is suspended by the violent force of the trouble. This is felt most in sudden distresses that come over the soul like a torrent or a flash flood, and especially in bodily illnesses. Because of the close bond between soul and body, these affect the soul so much that they hinder not only its spiritual activity but often its natural activity too. That is why Saint James tells us to pray ourselves when we are afflicted, but to send for the elders when we are sick (James 5:14), so that they, like those in the Gospel, may bring the sick person to God in their prayers, since he cannot present his own case. That is why God accepts a plea based on the sharpness and bitterness of the trouble, as with David in Psalm 6 and elsewhere. The Lord knoweth whereof we are made, he remembereth we are but dust (Psalm 103:14);

and that our strength is not the strength of steel. It is part of His faithfulness to us as His creatures, which is why He is called a faithful Creator (1 Peter 4:19). God is faithful, who will not suffer us to be tempted above that we are able (1 Corinthians 10:13). There were certain commandments the Jews called the hedges of the law. For example, to fence people off from cruelty, He commanded that they should not take the mother bird with the young, nor boil a kid in its mother’s milk (Exodus 23:19), nor muzzle the ox (1 Corinthians 9:9). Does God care for animals and not for His nobler creature? So we ought to judge charitably the complaints wrung from God’s people in such cases. Job was counted by God as a patient man in spite of those passionate complaints. Faith that is overwhelmed for the moment will regain its ground. And grief for sin, though it falls short of grief for misery in violence, goes beyond it in constancy, just as a running stream fed by a spring keeps flowing when a brook suddenly swollen by rain dries up.

To conclude this point, and to encourage us to a thorough work of bruising and to patience when God bruises us, let everyone know that no one is fitter for comfort than those who think themselves furthest from it. Most people do not feel lost enough to want a Saviour. A holy despair of ourselves is the ground of true hope (Hosea 14:3). In God the fatherless find mercy; if people were more fatherless, they would feel more of God’s fatherly affection from heaven. For God, who dwells in the highest heavens, also dwells in the lowliest soul (Isaiah 66:2). Christ’s sheep are weak sheep, lacking in one thing or another, so He attends to the needs of every sheep. He seeks what was lost, brings back what was driven away, binds up what was broken, and strengthens the weak (Ezekiel 34:16). His tenderest care is for the weakest. He carries the lambs in His bosom (Isaiah 40:11): Peter, feed my lambs. He was most approachable and open with troubled souls. How careful He was after His resurrection that Peter and the rest of the apostles should not be too downcast! Go tell the disciples, and tell Peter (Mark 16:7). Christ knew that the guilt of their unkindness in deserting Him had crushed their spirits. How gently He bore with Thomas’s unbelief, stooping so low to his weakness as to let him thrust his hand into His side!

fields.title: Grace Is Small at First
fields.body_html:
NOW for the second branch: God will not quench the smoking flax, or wick, but will fan it until it bursts into flame. In smoking flax there is only a little light, and that light is weak, since it cannot flame, and the little there is is mixed with smoke.

From this we observe, first, that in God’s children, especially at their first conversion, there is only a small amount of grace, and that little is mixed with much corruption, which, like smoke, is offensive. Secondly, that Christ will not quench this smoking flax.

First, grace is small at the beginning. Christians come in different ages: some are babies, some young men. Grace is like a grain of mustard seed (Matthew 17:20). Nothing is so small as grace at first, and nothing more glorious afterward. The things of greatest perfection take the longest to reach their full growth. Man, the most perfect creature, comes to perfection little by little. Worthless things, like mushrooms, or like Jonah’s gourd, spring up quickly and vanish quickly. A new creature is the most excellent thing in all the world, and so it grows up by degrees. We see in nature that a mighty oak grows from an acorn. It is with a Christian as it was with Christ, who sprang out of the dead stump of Jesse, out of David’s family, when it was at its lowest (Isaiah 53:2), yet He grew higher than the heavens. It is not with the trees of righteousness as it was with the trees of Paradise, which were all created perfect at the start. At the beginning the seeds of all the creatures in this beautiful world were hidden in the chaos, in that confused mass, out of which God commanded all creatures to rise. The trunk and branches, bud and fruit, all lie hidden in the small seeds of plants. All the comforting conclusions of holy truth lie hidden in a few first principles. All those glorious fireworks of zeal and holiness in the saints began from a few sparks.

So let us not be discouraged by the small beginnings of grace, but look on ourselves as chosen to be blameless and without spot (Ephesians 1:4). Let us look at our imperfect beginning only to spur ourselves on to strive further toward perfection and to keep us humble. Otherwise, when we are discouraged, we must look at ourselves as Christ does, who sees us as those He intends to make fit for Himself. Christ values us by what we shall be and by what we are chosen for. We call a little plant a tree because it is growing up to become one. Who hath despised the day of small things? (Zechariah 4:10). Christ would not have us despise little things.

The glorious angels do not scorn to wait on little ones, little in their own eyes and little in the eyes of the world.

Grace, though little in quantity, is great in strength and worth.

It is Christ who raises the worth of small and lowly places and people. Bethlehem was the least (Micah 5:2; Matthew 2:6), and yet not the least: the least in itself, but not the least, since Christ was born there. The second temple (Haggai 2:9) fell short of the outward magnificence of the first, yet it was more glorious than the first because Christ came into it. The Lord of the temple came into His own temple. The pupil of the eye is very small, yet it sees a large part of the sky at once. A pearl, though small, is highly valued. Nothing in the world is as useful as the smallest drop of grace.

fields.title: Grace Is Mixed with Corruption
fields.body_html:
BUT grace is not only small; it is mixed with corruption. That is why a Christian is said to be smoking flax. From this we see that grace does not destroy corruption all at once; some is left to struggle against. The purest actions of the purest people need Christ to perfume them, and that is His office. When we pray, we need to pray again for Christ to pardon the defects of our prayers. Look at some examples of this smoking flax. Moses at the Red Sea, in great perplexity and not knowing what to say or which way to turn, groaned to God. No doubt there was a great conflict in him. In great distress we do not know what to pray, but the Spirit makes request with sighs that cannot be expressed (Romans 8:26). Broken hearts can produce only broken prayers.

When David was before the king of Gath (1 Samuel 21) and disfigured himself in an undignified way, there was some fire in that smoke too. You may see what an excellent psalm he wrote on that occasion, in which he says from experience, The Lord is near unto them that are of a contrite spirit (Psalm 34:18). I said in my haste, I am cast out of thy sight: there is smoke. Yet thou heardest the voice of my prayer (Psalm 31:22): there is fire. Master, carest thou not that we perish? (Matthew 8:25), cry the disciples. Here is the smoke of unbelief, yet enough light of faith to stir them up to pray to Christ. Lord, I believe: there is light. But help my unbelief (Mark 9:24): there is smoke.

Jonah cries, I am cast out of thy sight (Jonah 2:4): there is smoke. Yet will I look again to thy holy temple: there is light.

O wretched man that I am (Romans 7:24), says Saint Paul, feeling his corruption; and yet he breaks out into thanks to God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

I sleep, says the Church in the Song of Songs, but my heart waketh (Song 5:2). Of the seven churches, which for their light are called seven golden lampstands (Revelation 2 and 3), most had a great deal of smoke with their light.

The reason for this mixture is that we carry two principles within us, grace and nature. Its purpose is especially to keep us from the two dangerous rocks our nature is prone to crash on, complacency and pride, and to force us to rest on justification, not on sanctification, which besides being imperfect also carries some stain.

Our spiritual fire is like our ordinary fire down here: it is mixed. But fire is purest in its own element above. So all our graces will be when we are where we long to be, in heaven, which is our proper element.

This mixture is why God’s people judge themselves so differently, looking sometimes at the work of grace and sometimes at the corruption that remains. When they look at the corruption, they think they have no grace. Though they love Christ in His ordinances and His children, they do not dare claim so close an acquaintance as to be His. Just as a candle burning down in its holder sometimes shows its light and sometimes seems to lose it, so they are sometimes well assured about themselves and sometimes at a loss.

fields.title: Christ Will Not Quench Small and Weak Beginnings
fields.body_html:
NOW for the second observation: Christ will not quench the smoking flax. First, because this spark is from heaven; it is His own, lit by His own Spirit. Secondly, because it serves the glory of His powerful grace in His children that He keeps light alive in the middle of darkness, a spark in the middle of the swelling waters of corruption.

There is a special blessing in that little spark. When new wine is found in the cluster, one says, Destroy it not; for a blessing is in it (Isaiah 65:8). We see how our Saviour Christ bore with Thomas in his doubting (John 20:27), and with the two disciples going to Emmaus, who wavered over whether He had come to redeem Israel or not (Luke 24:21). He did not quench the little light in Peter, which was smothered. Peter denied Him, but He did not deny Peter (Matthew 26). If thou wilt, thou canst, said one poor man in the Gospel (Matthew 8:2). If thou canst, said another. Both were smoking flax, and neither was quenched. If Christ had stood on His own greatness, He would have rejected the man who came with his “if”; but Christ answers his “if” with a gracious and absolute grant: I will; be thou clean. The woman with the issue of blood only touched Him, and with a trembling hand, and only the hem of His garment, and yet she went away both healed and comforted. In the seven churches (Revelation 2 and 3) we see that He acknowledges and cherishes anything good in them. Because the disciples slept from weakness, weighed down by grief, our Saviour Christ makes a comforting excuse for them: the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak (Matthew 26:41).

If Christ were not merciful, He would miss His own goals: there is forgiveness with thee, that thou mayest be feared. Now everyone is willing to come under the banner of love He spreads over His people; therefore unto thee shall all flesh come (Psalm 65:2). He uses restraint and care, lest the spirit should fail before Him, and the souls which He has made (Isaiah 57:16). The text says Christ’s heart was moved with compassion when He saw them without food, lest they should faint. Much more will He take care to prevent our spiritual fainting.

Here see how opposite the holy nature of Christ is to the impure nature of man. Man will quench the light because of a little smoke; Christ, we see, always cherishes even the smallest beginnings.

How He bore with the many imperfections of His poor disciples! If He rebuked them sharply, it was in love, so that they might shine more brightly. Could we have a better pattern to follow than that of the One by whom we hope to be saved? We then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak (Romans 15:1). I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some (1 Corinthians 9:22). Oh, that this winning, gaining spirit were in more people! Many are lost, as far as it depends on us, for lack of encouragement. See how that faithful fisher of men, Saint Paul, works to catch his judge: I know that thou believest the prophets (Acts 26:27). Then he wishes him every saving good, except the chains. He might have wished him those too, but he would not discourage someone who had made only a start, so he wished Agrippa only what was good in religion. How careful our blessed Saviour was that little ones should not be made to stumble (Matthew 12 and 13). How He defends His disciples from the malicious accusations of the Pharisees! How careful He is not to put new wine into old wineskins (Matthew 9:17), not to put off new beginners with the hardships of religion, as some unwisely do. Oh, He says, they will have time to fast when I am gone, and strength to fast when the Holy Spirit has come on them.

It is not the best way to come down hard at once on young beginners for some lesser vanities. Show them a more excellent way, build them up on positive foundations, and other things will soon lose their appeal for them. It is not wrong to cover their shortcomings, to excuse some failings, to praise what they do well, to encourage their willingness, to remove every obstacle from their path, and to help them in every way to bear the yoke of religion more easily, bringing them to love God and His service, so that they do not develop a distaste for it before they know it. Usually we see Christ plant in young beginners a love we call the first love (Revelation 2:4), to carry them through their profession with more delight; and He does not expose them to hardships before they have gathered strength, just as we raise young plants and shield them from the weather until they have taken root. Mercy toward others should often move us to give up our lawful freedoms when they would cause weak ones to stumble. It is the little ones who are made to stumble (Matthew 18:6). The weakest are the most likely to think they are despised, so we should take the greatest care to satisfy them. It would be a good contest among Christians for one to work at giving no offence and the other to work at taking none. The best people are strict with themselves and tender toward others.

Yet people should not tire out and wear down the patience of others. Nor should the weaker demand so much gentleness from others that they lean on that indulgence and settle down in their own weaknesses, to the danger of their own souls and the scandal of the church.

Nor, because of this, should they make light of God’s gifts in others, which grace teaches us to honour wherever they are found. They should know their abilities and their place, and not undertake anything beyond their measure that might expose both themselves and their cause to scorn. When blindness and boldness, ignorance and arrogance, weakness and wilfulness meet in one person, it makes him hateful to God, burdensome in company, dangerous in his advice, a troubler of better plans, unmanageable and incapable of better direction, and miserable in the end. When Christ shows His gracious power in weakness, He does it by letting people understand themselves well enough to breed humility and to magnify God’s love to such as they are. He does it as a safeguard against being discouraged by weakness, since weakness brings people nearer to grace, being a help toward poverty of spirit, than greatness of position and gifts, which give corrupt nature fuel for pride. Christ refuses no one for weakness of gifts, so that no one should be discouraged; and He accepts no one for greatness, so that no one should be puffed up by what counts for so little with God. It does not matter much how dull the pupil is when Christ takes on the role of teacher; for as He prescribes what to understand, He also gives understanding itself, even to the simplest.

The church suffers a good deal from weak ones, so we may claim the freedom to deal with them not only gently but often directly. The aim of true love is to make the person better, and keeping quiet often hinders that. With some, a spirit of gentleness works best; with others, a rod. Some must be pulled out of the fire with force (Jude 23), and they will bless God for us on the day of their visitation. We see our Saviour heap woe upon woe when He had to deal with hard-hearted hypocrites (Matthew 23). For hypocrites need stronger conviction than open sinners, because their will is corrupt, and so their conversion is usually violent. A hard knot needs a matching wedge; otherwise, in a cruel kind of pity, we betray their souls. A sharp rebuke is sometimes a precious pearl and a sweet balm. The wounds of complacent sinners will not be healed with sweet words. The Holy Spirit came in tongues of fire as well as in the likeness of a dove; and the same Holy Spirit will grant a spirit of prudence and discretion, which is the salt that seasons all our words and actions. Such wisdom will teach us to speak a word in season (Isaiah 50:4), both to the weary and to the complacent soul. Indeed, whoever is to raise up or cast down needs the tongue of the learned. But in this place I am speaking of gentleness toward those who are weak and feel it. These we must lead on gently and drive slowly, as Jacob did his cattle (Genesis 33:14), at their own pace, and as his children were able to bear.

Weak Christians are like glasses, which are damaged by the least rough handling but last a long time if handled gently. We are to give this honour of gentle handling to the weaker vessels (1 Peter 3:7). By it we will both preserve them and make them useful to the church and to ourselves.

In unhealthy bodies, if you purge out all the bad humours, you will purge out life and all. So although God says He will refine them as silver is refined (Zechariah 13:9), yet in Isaiah 48:10 He says He has refined them, but not as silver; that is, not so thoroughly that no dross remains, for He takes our weakness into account. Perfect refining is for another world, the world of the spirits of just men made perfect.

fields.title: Tenderness Required in Ministers toward Young Beginners
fields.body_html:
SO ministers need to be careful how they deal with these people in several particulars. First, let them be careful not to set the bar too high, making things into general and necessary evidences of grace that do not fit the experience of many a good Christian, and hanging salvation and damnation on things not fit to bear such great weight. In that way people are cast down without cause, lower than they can quickly be raised up again by themselves or others. The ambassadors of so gentle a Saviour should not be too domineering, setting themselves up in people’s hearts where Christ alone should sit, as in His own temple. Too much regard for man was one of the ways the papal system crept in. Let a man so account of us, as of the ministers of Christ (1 Corinthians 4:1): neither more nor less, just that much. How careful St. Paul was in cases of conscience not to lay a trap for any weak conscience!

They should also be careful not to hide their meaning in obscure speech, talking in the clouds. Truth fears nothing so much as being hidden, and wants nothing so much as to be laid open clearly to everyone’s view. When it is most bare, it is most lovely and powerful.

Our blessed Saviour, as He took our nature on Himself, also took on our everyday way of speaking, which was part of His voluntary humbling. St. Paul was a profound man, yet he became like a nurse to the weaker sort (1 Thessalonians 2:7).

The spirit of mercy that was in Christ should move His servants to be willing to lower themselves for the good of the lowliest. Why did the kingdom of heaven suffer violence after John the Baptist’s time (Matthew 11:12), except that comforting truths were laid open with such plainness and clarity that people were so moved by them that they did a holy violence to take hold of them?

Christ chose those who had felt the most mercy to preach mercy, such as St. Peter and St. Paul, so that they might be examples of what they taught. St. Paul became all things to all men (1 Corinthians 9:22), stooping to them for their good. Christ came down from heaven and emptied Himself of majesty in tender love for souls; shall we not come down from our lofty opinions to do any poor soul good? Shall man be proud after God has been humble? We see the ministers of Satan turn themselves into every shape to make converts (Matthew 23:15). A Jesuit will be all things to every man. We see ambitious men study how to fit themselves to the moods of those by whom they hope to be promoted. And shall we not study how to fit ourselves to Christ, by whom we hope to be raised up, and with whom we are in fact already sitting in heavenly places? After we have been won to Christ ourselves, we should work to win others to Christ. A holy ambition and a holy covetousness will move us to put on the disposition of Christ; but we must first put off ourselves.

Thirdly, we should not rack their minds with intricate or doubtful disputes (Romans 14:1), for in that way we will distract and tire them and give them a reason to throw off all care. The age of the church most fertile in subtle questions was the most barren in religion, because such questions make people think religion is only a matter of cleverness, of tying and untying knots. People whose minds run that way usually have hotter heads than hearts.

Nevertheless, when we are cast into times and places where doubts are raised about main points, people ought to work to be firmly grounded. God often allows questions to arise to test our love and exercise our abilities. Nothing is so certain as what is certain after doubts. Shaking settles and roots. In a quarrelsome age it takes real understanding to be a Christian and to know what to rest one’s soul on. Here it is an office of love to remove the stones and smooth the way to heaven. So we must take care that, on the pretext of avoiding disputes, we do not let an opposing party gain ground on the truth, for in this way we may easily betray both the truth of God and the souls of men.

Those also fall short who drive troubled souls away from finding comfort with them by too much severity. Because of this behaviour, many people smother their temptations and burn inwardly, because they have no one to whom they can pour out their grief and ease their souls.

We must neither bind where God looses, nor loose where God binds, nor open where God shuts, nor shut where God opens. The right use of the keys always succeeds. In applying truth to individuals, great care must be taken. A man may be a false prophet and yet speak the truth, if it is not a truth for the person he is speaking to. If he grieves those whom God has not grieved, by truths at the wrong time, or offers comfort in the wrong way, the hearts of the wicked may be strengthened. One man’s meat may be another man’s poison.

If we look at the general mood of these times, rousing and awakening scriptures are the most fitting; yet there are many broken spirits who need soft and soothing words. Even in the worst times the prophets mixed in sweet comfort for the hidden remnant of faithful people. God has Comfort ye my people (Isaiah 40:1) as well as Lift up thy voice like a trumpet (Isaiah 58:1).

And here too a warning is needed. Mercy does not rob us of right judgment, so that we take stinking firebrands for smoking flax. No one will demand more mercy from others than those who deserve severity. This example does not approve lukewarmness, or too much indulgence toward those who need stirring up. Cold diseases need hot remedies. It was to the church at Ephesus’s just praise that it could not bear them which are evil (Revelation 2:2). We should bear with others in such a way that we also show our dislike of evil. Our Saviour Christ would not hold back sharp rebuke where He saw dangerous weaknesses, even in His most beloved disciples. It brings a curse to do the work of the Lord negligently (Jeremiah 48:10), even when it is a work of just severity, such as plunging the sword into the enemy’s body. And those whom we allow to be betrayed by their worst enemies, their sins, will have good reason to curse us one day.

It is hard to keep the right balance between mercy and severity without a spirit above our own, by which we ought to desire to be led in everything. That wisdom which dwells with prudence (Proverbs 8:12) will guide us in these particulars; without it, virtue is not virtue and truth is not truth. The rule and the case must be laid side by side, for without close insight, an apparent likeness between situations will breed errors in our judgment of them. Those fiery, stormy and destructive spirits in the papal system who try to promote their religion by cruelty show that they are strangers to the wisdom from above, which makes people gentle, peaceable and ready to show others the mercy they have felt themselves. Winning through some patience and moderation is a way of prevailing that suits Christ, and suits human nature too.

And yet we often see a false spirit in those who call for moderation. They do it only to push their own plans with greater strength; and if they end up on the winning side, they will hardly show others the moderation they now demand from others. There is also a proud kind of moderation, when people take it on themselves to criticize both sides, as if they were wiser than both; although, if the spirit is right, an onlooker may see more than those who are in the fight.

fields.title: Those Who Govern Should Be Tender toward Weak Ones, and So Should Private Christians
fields.body_html:
SO in the church’s discipline, it is more in keeping with the spirit of Christ to lean toward the milder side, and not to kill a fly on someone’s forehead with a sledgehammer, or shut people out of heaven over a trifle. Even the snuffers of the tabernacle were made of pure gold, to show how pure that discipline should be by which the church’s light is kept bright. The power given to the church is given for building up, not for destruction. How careful St. Paul was that the repentant incestuous Corinthian should not be swallowed up with too much grief (2 Corinthians 2:7)! As for civil magistrates, for civil necessities and reasons of state they must let the law take its course; yet they should imitate this gentle king at least so far as not to mix bitterness and passion with the authority they have from God. Authority is a beam of God’s majesty, and it prevails most where there is least mixture of what is merely human. It takes more than ordinary wisdom to handle it rightly. This string must not be wound too tight, nor let too loose. Justice is a matter of harmony. Herbs that are hot or cold beyond a certain degree kill. We see even opposite elements kept together in one body by wise balancing. Justice applied with full rigour is often extreme injustice, where significant circumstances should incline us to moderation; and the reckoning will be easier for leaning toward moderation than toward rigour.

Insolent behaviour toward miserable people, once they are humbled, is unbecoming in anyone who looks for mercy himself. Misery should be a magnet for mercy, not a footstool for pride to trample on.

Sometimes it happens that those under the government of others do the most harm by contrariness and harsh criticism, belittling and discouraging the efforts of those over them for the public good. Given how weak human nature is, and especially in this cracked and failing age of the world, we ought to take in good part whatever moderate happiness we enjoy through government, and not be like a nail in the wound, making things worse by misinterpreting them. Here love should have a cloak to throw over the lesser errors of those above us. Often the poor man becomes the oppressor through unjust outcry. We should work to put the best interpretation on the actions of those who govern that the nature of the actions can possibly bear.

Finally, there is something here for private Christians to note, indeed for all of us in our ordinary relationships: we owe the weak many things.

1. Let us be watchful in how we use our freedom, and work to be inoffensive in our conduct, so that our example does not force them. An example has commanding power, as Peter’s did (Galatians 2). A loose life is cruelty to ourselves and to the souls of others. Though we cannot keep those from perishing who will perish, as far as the outcome goes, yet if we do what by its nature tends to destroy the souls of others, their ruin is charged to us.

2. Let people beware of taking up Satan’s office by twisting the good actions of others, as he did Job’s: Doth Job fear God for nought? Or by slandering them, judging them by the wickedness in their own hearts. The devil gains more by such discouragements, and by the insults thrown at religion, than by fire and the stake. Like untimely frosts, these nip every gracious beginning in the bud, and do all they can, like Herod, to kill Christ in young believers. A Christian is a holy and sacred thing, Christ’s temple; and whoever destroys His temple, Christ will destroy (1 Corinthians 3:17).

3. Among the things to beware of, there is among private Christians a bold assumption of the right to judge others without considering their temptations. Some will, in a temper, cut others off from the church and the brotherhood. But disorders do not change true relationships. Though a child in a fit of temper should disown its mother, the mother will not disown the child.

So in these judgmental times there is good reason for St. James’s warning that there should not be too many masters (James 3:1), and that we should not strike one another with hasty judgments, especially in matters that are neither commanded nor forbidden. Some things depend on the mind of the person who does them or does not do them, for both may be done unto the Lord.

A holy aim in matters of this middle kind makes people’s judgments, even when they seem to contradict each other, not so much to blame. Because of the good aims He sees in us, Christ overlooks any wrong in them so far as not to charge it against us.

People must not be too inquisitive in prying into the weaknesses of others. We should work instead to see what they have that is for eternity, to incline our hearts to love them, rather than looking into the weakness that God’s Spirit will in time consume, which only estranges us. Some think it is strength of grace to put up with nothing in the weaker, whereas the strongest are the readiest to bear with the weaknesses of the weak.

Where there is most holiness, there is most moderation, as far as that can be without harm to godliness toward God and to the good of others. In this text we see in Christ a wonderful combination of absolute holiness and great moderation. What would have become of our salvation if He had stood on His terms and not stooped this low to us? We need not try to be holier than Christ. It is no flattery to do as He does, as long as it is for building up.

The Holy Spirit is willing to live in smoky, offensive souls. Oh, that the Spirit would breathe the same merciful disposition into our spirits! We put up with the bitterness of wormwood and other unpleasant plants and herbs only because we know from experience that they have some healthy property. Why then should we reject people of useful gifts and graces just for some harshness of temperament, which, as much as it offends us, grieves them too?

While we live here, grace is in souls which are only imperfectly renewed, and which live in bodies subject to various humours that sometimes incline the soul to excess in one passion and sometimes in another.

Bucer was a deep and moderate theologian. After long experience he resolved to refuse no one in whom he saw (aliquid Christi) something of Christ.

In this imperfect state the best Christians are like gold coins slightly under weight, which need a few grains of allowance to make them pass. You must give the best their allowance. We must make up, out of our love and mercy, what we see lacking in them.

The church of Christ is a common hospital, in which everyone is to some degree sick with one spiritual disease or another, so that we all have reason to exercise the spirit of wisdom and gentleness toward each other.

To do this better, let us put on the spirit of Christ. The Spirit of God carries a majesty with Him. Corruption will hardly give way to corruption in another; pride cannot stand pride. The weapons of this warfare must not be worldly (2 Corinthians 10:4). The great apostles would not start the work of ministry until they were clothed, as it were, with power from on high (Luke 24:49). The Spirit will work only with His own tools. And we should think about what feeling Christ would have toward the person in this case. That great Physician, as He had a quick eye and a healing tongue, also had a gentle hand and a tender heart.

Secondly, put ourselves in the place of the person we are dealing with. We are, or have been, or may be like them. Make the case our own, and also consider how close a relationship a Christian has with us: a brother, a fellow member, an heir of the same salvation. So let us take tender care of them in every way, and especially in protecting the peace of their consciences. Conscience is a tender and delicate thing, and must be treated as such. It is like a lock: if the wards are disturbed, it will be hard to open.

fields.title: Rules for Testing Whether We Are Such as Christ Will Not Quench
fields.body_html:
NOW for a test, to let us see whether we are this smoking flax that Christ will not quench. In this test, remember these: 1. Rules. 2. Signs.

1. We must have two eyes: one to see imperfections in ourselves and others, the other to see what is good. I am black, says the church, but comely. Those who are always quarrelling with themselves never find comfort; through their weaknesses they are inclined to feed on bitter things that most nourish the very disorders they are sick with. They like to look only at the dark side of the cloud.

2. We must not always judge ourselves by our present feelings, because in temptations we will see nothing but the smoke of distrustful thoughts. Fire may be banked up in the ashes even though it cannot be seen; in winter, life is hidden in the root.

3. Beware of false reasoning, such as concluding that because our fire does not blaze as others’ do, we have no fire at all. By false conclusions like that we come to sin against the commandment by bearing false witness against ourselves. The prodigal did not say he was no son, but that he was not worthy to be called a son (Luke 15:19). We must neither trust false evidence nor deny true evidence. Otherwise we would dishonour the work of God’s Spirit in us and lose the help of the evidence that would nourish our love for Christ and arm us against Satan’s discouragements. Some are so much at fault here that it is as if Satan, the accuser of the brethren (Revelation 12:10), had hired them to plead his case by accusing themselves.

4. As a foundation for this, know that in the covenant of grace God requires grace to be genuine, not any set amount of it; and a spark of fire is fire just as much as a whole furnace. So we must look for grace in the spark as well as in the flame. Not everyone has an equally strong faith, but all have an equally precious faith (2 Peter 1:1), by which they lay hold of and put on the perfect righteousness of Christ. A weak hand may receive a rich jewel. A few grapes will show that the plant is a vine and not a thornbush. It is one thing to be lacking in grace and another to lack grace altogether. God knows we have nothing of our own, so in the covenant of grace He requires no more than He gives; He gives what He requires, and He accepts what He gives. Whoever does not have a lamb may bring a pair of turtledoves (Leviticus 12:8). What is the Gospel itself but a merciful moderation, in which Christ’s obedience is counted as ours and our sins are laid on Him, and in which God, instead of a judge, becomes a father, pardoning our sins and accepting our obedience, feeble and flawed as it is? Under the covenant of grace we are now brought to heaven by a way of love and mercy.

It will be a special help to know clearly the difference between the covenant of works and the covenant of grace, between Moses and Christ. Moses, without any mercy, breaks every bruised reed and quenches all smoking flax. For the law requires obedience that is 1. personal, 2. perpetual, 3. perfect, 4. and from a perfect heart, and all under a most terrible curse; and it gives no strength. It is a harsh slave-driver, like Pharaoh’s, demanding the full quota of bricks while giving no straw. Christ comes with blessing after blessing even on those whom Moses had cursed, and with healing balm for the wounds Moses had made.

The same duties are required in both covenants, such as loving the Lord with all our heart, with all our soul and so on (Deuteronomy 6:5). In the covenant of works this must be taken in its full strictness; but under the covenant of grace it means a sincere effort in proportion to the grace received. That is how we must understand it when it is said of Josiah and others that they loved God with all their hearts. It must be softened in the gospel’s way.

The law is sweetened by the Gospel and becomes delightful to the inner man (Romans 7:22). Under this gracious covenant, sincerity is perfection. This is the death in the pot in the Roman religion, that it confuses the two covenants. And it kills the comfort of drooping souls that they cannot tell the two apart. So they let themselves be held in bondage (Isaiah 61:1–2) when Christ has set them free, and they stay in the prison when Christ has opened the doors in front of them.

5. Grace is sometimes so small that we cannot detect it. The Spirit sometimes works secretly in us in ways we are not aware of at the time; but Christ knows. Sometimes, in the bitterness of temptation, when the Spirit is struggling with a sense of God’s anger, we are inclined to think God is our enemy. A troubled soul is like troubled water: we can see nothing in it, and as long as it is not cleansed, it will throw up mud and dirt. It is full of objections against itself. Yet usually we can detect something of this hidden life and these smothered sparks.

On a gloomy day there is enough light for us to know it is day and not night. In the same way there is something in a Christian under a cloud by which he can be recognized as a true believer and not a hypocrite. In the state of grace there is never pure darkness, but always some beam of light, so that the kingdom of darkness does not entirely prevail.

fields.title: Signs of Smoking Flax That Christ Will Not Quench
fields.body_html:
WITH these things laid down first, let us know, as a test: First, if there is any holy fire in us, it is lit from heaven by the Father of lights, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness (2 Corinthians 4:6). As it is lit through the use of means, so it is fed by them. The light in us and the light in the word spring from each other, and both from the Holy Spirit. So when people pay no attention to the word, it is because there is no light in them (Isaiah 8:20). Heavenly truths need a heavenly light to see them. Natural people see heavenly things, but not in their own proper light, only by a lower light. In every converted person God puts a light into the eye of the soul in proportion to the light of the truths revealed to him. A worldly eye will never see spiritual things.

Secondly, the smallest divine light has some warmth with it. Light in the understanding produces the warmth of love in the affections. To the degree that the sanctified understanding sees something to be true or good, the will embraces it. Weak light produces weak inclinations; strong light, strong inclinations. A little spiritual light is strong enough to answer strong objections from flesh and blood, and to see through all earthly attractions and opposing obstacles, showing them to be far inferior to the heavenly things it has its eye on.

All light that is not spiritual gives way to every little temptation, because it lacks the strength of sanctifying grace, especially when the temptation is shaped to fit a person’s own inclinations. That is why Christians whose light is small in quantity but heavenly in quality hold out when people with broader understanding sink.

Light wins out in the soul like this because in the godly, together with the spirit of illumination, there goes a spirit of power (2 Timothy 1:7) to bring the heart under the truth revealed, and to give the will a taste and relish that matches the sweetness of the truths. Otherwise a merely natural will rises up against supernatural truths, having an aversion and hostility toward them. In the godly, holy truths come by way of taste; gracious people have a spiritual palate as well as a spiritual eye. Grace changes what we relish. Thirdly, where this heavenly light is lit, it directs us in the right way. That is what it is given for: to show us the best way and to guide us through the particular situations of life. If it does not, it is only common light, given only for the good of others. Some have the light of knowledge yet do not follow that light, but are guided by worldly reasoning and scheming. The prophet speaks of such people: Behold, all ye that kindle a fire, walk in the light of your fire, and in the sparks that ye have kindled. This shall ye have of mine hand; ye shall lie down in sorrow (Isaiah 50:11). God delights to confound worldly wisdom as hostile to Him and as robbing Him of His prerogative, who alone is the only wise God. So we must walk by His light and not by the blaze of our own fire. God must light our candle (Psalm 18:28), or we are likely to stay in darkness. Sparks not lit from heaven are not strong enough to keep us from lying down in sorrow, though they make a bigger blaze and show than the light from above. Just as madmen do greater things than sane people, but by a false strength, so the excess of these people’s joy comes from a false light. The candle of the wicked shall be put out.

The light some people have is like lightning, which after a sudden flash leaves them in deeper darkness. They can love the light as it shines, but hate it when it exposes and directs. A little holy light will enable a person to keep the word, and not betray religion or deny Christ’s name, as Christ says of the church at Philadelphia (Revelation 3:8).

Fourthly, where this fire is, it will separate things of different natures and show the difference between them, as between gold and dross. It will separate flesh from spirit and show that this is from nature and that from grace. Not everything in a bad action is bad, nor everything in a good action good. There is gold in the ore, which God and His Spirit in us can tell apart. A worldly person’s heart is like a dungeon where nothing can be seen but horror and confusion. This light makes us discerning and humble, through a clearer sight of God’s purity and our own uncleanness, and it enables us to recognize the work of the Spirit in another person.

Fifthly, to the extent that someone is spiritual, light is delightful to him. He is willing to see anything that is wrong so that he may correct it, and any further service revealed so that he may do it, because he truly hates evil and loves good. If he goes against light that has been shown him, he will soon be brought back, because the light has an ally inside him. So at the first sight of his error he is quickly open to advice, as David was when he intended to kill Nabal, and he blesses God afterward for being stopped on a bad path (1 Samuel 25:32).

In a worldly person the light breaks in on him, but he works to block the openings; he has no delight in coming to the light. Before the Spirit of grace has subdued the heart, it is impossible for it not to sin against the light. It resists it, or keeps it prisoner under base desires, burying it, as it were, in the earth; or it twists it, making it an agent and servant of the flesh, searching out arguments to defend the flesh; or it misuses the little light it has to keep out a greater, higher and more heavenly light, and so at last makes the light it has a misleading guide into utter darkness. The reason is that the light has no friend inside; the soul is turned the opposite way. And light always disturbs the sinful peace people are eager to speak to themselves. That is why we see it often enrage people all the more, just as the spring sun breeds feverish illnesses because it stirs up the humours without dispersing them. Nothing in the world is more restless than the heart of a wicked person who sits under the means of knowledge, until, like a thief, he puts out the candle so that he can sin with less check. Spiritual light is distinct: it sees spiritual good and applies it to ourselves. Common light is confused and lets sin lie undisturbed. Where there is fire in any degree, it will fight against what is opposed to it. From the beginning God put irreconcilable hatred between light and darkness, and so between good and evil, flesh and spirit (Galatians 5:17). Grace will never join with sin, any more than fire with water. Fire will mix with nothing opposed to it but keeps its own purity, and is never corrupted as the other elements are. So those who argue and scheme for the freedoms of the flesh show that they are strangers to the life of God. Because of this conflict, gracious people often complain that they have no grace. But they contradict themselves in their complaints, as if someone who can see should complain that he cannot see, or complain that he is asleep, when the very complaint, springing from displeasure at sin, shows that there is something in him opposed to sin. Can a dead person complain? Some things, though bad in themselves, reveal something good, as smoke reveals some fire. A rash breaking out on the body shows the strength of nature. Some weaknesses reveal more good than some apparently beautiful actions. Excessive passion in opposing evil, though it cannot be justified, shows a better spirit than a calm temper when there is good reason to be moved. It is better for the water to run somewhat muddy than not to run at all. Job had more grace in his disorders than his friends had in their apparently wise behaviour. Actions stained with some weaknesses are more acceptable than performances done merely for show.

Fire, even in the smallest amount, is to some degree active. So the smallest amount of grace is at work, since it springs from the Spirit of God, who because of His working nature is compared to fire. In fact, even in sins, when nothing seems active but corruption, there is an opposite principle that breaks the force of sin, so that it is not exceedingly sinful as it is in those who are worldly (Romans 7:13).

Fire makes metals pliable and malleable, and so does grace where it has begun: it works the heart into being pliable and ready for every good impression. Unmanageable spirits show that they are not even smoking flax.

Fire turns everything it can into fire. So grace works to produce the same impression in others and make as many good as it can. Grace also makes a gracious use even of natural and civil things and makes them spiritual. What another person does only as a citizen, a gracious person will do in a holy way. Whether he eats or drinks or whatever he does, he does it all to the glory of God, making everything serve the final goal.

Sparks naturally fly upward. So the spirit of grace carries the soul toward heaven and sets holy and heavenly aims before us. As it was lit from heaven, it carries us back to heaven. The part follows the whole: fire rises upward, and so does every spark, toward its own element. Where the aim and bent of the soul is toward God, there is grace, even if it is opposed. The smallest measure of it is holy desires springing from faith and love; for we cannot desire anything we do not first believe exists, and the desire for it comes from love. So desires are counted, to some degree, as part of the thing desired. But then they must be, first, constant, because constancy shows that they have become natural by supernatural means and are not forced. Secondly, they must be directed toward spiritual things, such as believing and loving God, not out of some special emergency, because people think that if they had grace now they might escape some danger, but in the way a loving heart is drawn to what it loves for some excellence in the thing itself. Thirdly, along with desire there is grief when it is hindered, which stirs us to prayer: O that my ways were directed to keep thy statutes! (Psalm 119:5). O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me? (Romans 7:24). Fourthly, desires keep pushing us onward: Oh that I might serve God with more freedom; oh that I were freer from these offensive, unsavoury, foul desires.

Fire, if it has anything to feed on, works its way into a larger area and rises higher and higher, and the higher it rises, the purer the flame. So where true grace is, it grows in measure and purity. Smoking flax will grow into a flame; and as it increases, it works out what is opposed to it and refines itself more and more. So it shows a false heart to set ourselves a limit in grace and to rest content with beginnings, pleading that Christ will not quench the smoking flax. But this merciful disposition in Christ is joined to perfect holiness, shown in His perfect hatred of sin. Rather than let sin go without its deserved punishment, He Himself became a sacrifice for sin, in which His Father’s holiness and His own shone most of all. Besides this, in the work of sanctification, though He favours His own work in us, He does not favour sin in us. He will never take His hand from His work until He has removed sin from our natures, even in its very existence. The same Spirit who purified that blessed human nature from which He was made cleanses us step by step to fit so holy a head, and He shapes the judgment and affections of all to whom He shows mercy to agree with His own, working to advance His purposes in removing sin from our nature.

fields.title: Doubts That Hinder Comfort Removed
fields.body_html:
MEDITATING on these rules and signs can bring much comfort into the souls of the weakest. So that it may come in greater abundance, let me add something to help them past a few common objections and secret thoughts against themselves, which, once they get inside the heart, often keep them down.

Some think they have no faith at all because they do not have full assurance, when even the finest fire there is will give off some smoke. The best actions will smell of smoke. A mortar in which garlic has been crushed will always smell of it; so all our actions will taste somewhat of the old man.

When their bodies are weak, some think grace is dying, because what they do is feeble, since their spirits, the instruments of the soul’s actions, are drained. They do not consider that God takes notice of the hidden sighs of those who lack the strength to express them outwardly. He who pronounces those blessed who consider the poor will Himself have merciful consideration for such people.

Others again are haunted by hideous images in their imagination, and by vile and unworthy thoughts of God, of Christ, of the word and so on, which disturb and harass their peace like swarming flies. These are thrown in like wildfire by Satan, as can be recognized by 1. their strangeness, 2. their strength and violence, 3. their horribleness, even to corrupt nature. A godly soul is no more guilty of them than Benjamin was of Joseph’s cup put into his sack. Among other remedies prescribed by godly writers, such as detesting them and turning from them to other things, let this be one: complain to Christ against them, fly under the wings of His protection, and ask Him to take our side against His enemy and ours. Shall every sin and blasphemy of man be forgiven, and not these blasphemous thoughts that have the devil for their father? Christ Himself was harassed in this way for this very reason, so that He might help all poor souls in the same situation.

But in this case there is a difference between Christ and us, because Satan had nothing of his own in Christ. His suggestions left no impression at all on Christ’s holy nature, but were put out at once, like sparks falling into the sea. Satan’s temptations of Christ were only suggestions on Satan’s part and a perception of their vileness on Christ’s part. To perceive evil suggested by someone else is not evil; it was Christ’s grief but Satan’s sin. He allowed Himself to be tempted in this way so that He might both pity us in our struggles and train us to handle our spiritual weapons as He did. Christ could have defeated Satan by power, but He did it by argument. When Satan comes to us, however, he finds something of his own in us that corresponds with him and keeps in touch with him. To some degree our nature has the same hostility toward God and goodness that is in Satan himself, and so his temptations usually leave some stain on us. Even if there were no devil to suggest them, sinful thoughts would still rise from within us. Though none were thrown in from outside, we have a mint of them inside. If the soul dwells on these thoughts long enough to draw any sinful pleasure from them, they leave a heavier guilt on the soul, hinder our sweet communion with God, interrupt our peace, put a contrary taste into the soul and dispose it to greater sins. All scandalous outbreaks are only thoughts at first. Evil thoughts are like little thieves who creep in at the window and open the door to bigger ones; thoughts are the seeds of actions. These thoughts, especially when Satan helps them along, make the life of many good Christians almost a martyrdom. In this situation some offer an unsound comfort: that evil thoughts arise from nature, and what is natural is excusable. But we must understand that nature, as it first came from God’s hands, had no such things rising out of it. The soul, as breathed into man by God, had no such foul breathings. But since it betrayed itself by sin, it has become in a sense natural to it to forge sinful imaginations and to be a furnace of such sparks. And this only makes the sinfulness of natural corruption worse, that it is so deeply rooted and so widely spread in our nature.

It helps our humility to know the whole breadth and depth of sin. Only this fact, that our nature, as far as it is unrenewed, is now so unhappily fruitful in evil thoughts, gives us this comfort: it is not our case alone, as if our condition here were different from everyone else’s. Some have been tempted to think so, almost to the point of despair: no one, they say, has such a loathsome nature as I do. This comes from not knowing how far original sin has spread; for what can come from an unclean thing but what is unclean? As in water face answereth to face, so the heart of man to man (Proverbs 27:19), where grace has not made some difference. As with attacks from Satan, so here the best way is to lay our complaints open to Christ and cry with Saint Paul, O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death? (Romans 7:24–25). As soon as he poured out his distressed soul like this, he found comfort, for he breaks into thanksgiving: I thank God, etc. And it is good to use this as an occasion to hate this foul body of death all the more and to draw nearer to God, as that holy man did after his foolish and beastly thoughts (Psalm 73:22, 28); and to keep our hearts closer to God, seasoning them with heavenly meditations in the morning, storing up good material so that our heart may be a good treasury, and begging Christ for His Holy Spirit to stop that cursed flow and to be a living spring of better thoughts in us. Nothing humbles the spirits of holy people more, people who want to delight in God after escaping the common pollutions of the world, than these unclean outflows of the spirit, because they are so contrary to God, who is a pure Spirit. But their very irksomeness gives us grounds for comfort against them. They drive the soul to every spiritual exercise, to watchfulness and to walking more closely with God, and to raising itself to thoughts of a higher kind, which the truth of God, the works of God, the communion of saints, the mystery of godliness, the thought of the terror of the Lord, and the excellence of a Christian’s state and the life that fits it, supply in abundance. They show us that we need daily cleansing and pardoning grace and need to seek to be found in Christ, and so they often bring the best of people to their knees.

But our chief comfort is this. Just as our blessed Saviour told Satan to get away from Him after He had put up with his impudence for a while (Matthew 4:10), so He will command him to leave us when it is good for us; he must go at a word.
