And in His own good time He can and will also rebuke the rebellious and wild stirrings of our hearts and bring all the thoughts of the inner man into submission to Himself.

Some think that because they have begun to be more troubled by the smoke of corruption than before, they must be worse than they were. It is true that their corruptions show more now than before, but they are less.

First, the more sin is seen, the more it is hated, and so the less it is. Specks of dust are in a room before the sun shines in, but only then do they show.

Secondly, the nearer opposites are to each other, the sharper the conflict between them. Of all enemies, the spirit and the flesh are nearest to each other, since both are in the soul of a regenerate person, in the faculties of the soul and in every action that springs from those faculties. So it is no wonder that the soul, the seat of this battle, divided against itself like this, should be like smoking flax.

Thirdly, the more grace, the more spiritual life; and the more spiritual life, the more aversion to what is opposed to it. So no one is as aware of corruption as those whose souls are most alive.

Fourthly, when people give themselves over to worldly freedoms, their corruptions do not trouble them, since they are not bound and tied up. But once grace holds back their wild and unrestrained excesses, the flesh boils, resenting being confined; and yet they are better now than they were before. The material that gives off smoke was in the torch before it was lit, but it does not offend until the torch begins to burn. Let such people know that if the smoke now offends them, it is a sign that there is light. It is better to enjoy the benefit of light, even with smoke, than to be entirely in the dark.

Nor is the smoke as offensive to us as the light is comforting, since the light gives evidence that there is true grace in the heart. So though it is troublesome in the conflict, it is comforting as evidence. It is better for corruption to offend us now than for us to buy a little peace by giving way to it, and lose our comfort later. So let those who are at war and at odds with their corruptions look on this text as their portion of comfort.

fields.title: Taking Up Duties in Spite of Weaknesses
fields.body_html:
HERE is an encouragement to duty: Christ will not quench the smoking flax but will fan it into flame. Some are reluctant to do good duties because they feel their hearts rebelling and their duties come out awkwardly. We should not avoid good actions because of the weaknesses that cling to them. Christ looks more at the good in them, which He means to cherish, than at the bad in them, which He means to abolish. A sick man will eat even though eating adds a little to his illness, so that his body may gain strength against the disease. In the same way, though sin clings to what we do, let us still do it, since we have to do with so good a Lord; and the more struggle we meet with, the more we are accepted. Christ loves to taste the good fruits that come from us, even though they will always taste of the old stock.

A Christian complains that he cannot pray: Oh, I am troubled with so many distracting thoughts, and never more than now. But has He put a desire to pray into your heart? He will hear the desires of His own Spirit in you. We know not what we should pray for as we ought (nor do we do anything else as we ought), but the Spirit helps our weaknesses with sighs and groans that cannot be expressed (Romans 8:26), which are not hidden from God. My groaning is not hid from thee (Psalm 38:9). God can make sense of a confused prayer. These desires cry louder in His ears than your sins. Sometimes a Christian’s thoughts are so confused that he can say nothing, but cries like a child, O Father, unable to show what it needs, as Moses did at the Red Sea.

These stirrings of the spirit touch God’s heart and melt Him into compassion toward us, when they come from the Spirit of adoption and from a striving to be better.

Oh, but the doubting heart thinks, is it possible that so holy a God should accept such a prayer?

Yes, He will accept what is His own and pardon what is ours. Jonah prayed in the belly of the fish, weighed down with the guilt of sin (Jonah 2:1), and yet God heard him. So let us not be discouraged by weaknesses. Saint James removes this objection.

Some might object: If I were as holy as Elijah, my prayers might be heard. But he says, Elias was a man subject to like passions as we are (James 5:17); he had his passions as well as we do. Do we think God heard him because he was without fault? Surely not. But let us look to the promises: call upon me in the day of trouble: I will deliver thee (Psalm 50:15); Ask, and it shall be given you (Matthew 7:7); and others like them. God accepts our prayers though they are weak: 1. because we are His own children, and they come from His own Spirit; 2. because they are according to His own will; 3. because they are offered through Christ’s mediation, and He takes them and mixes them with His own incense (Revelation 8:3). Not one holy sigh, not one tear we shed, is lost. And as every grace grows by being exercised, so does the grace of prayer; by praying we learn to pray. In the same way we should beware of a spirit of discouragement in all other holy duties, since we have so gracious a Saviour. Pray as we are able, listen as we are able, strive as we are able, do as we are able, according to the measure of grace we have received. God in Christ will look graciously on what is His own. Would Saint Paul do nothing because he could not do the good he wanted to? No, he pressed toward the mark (Philippians 3:14). Let us not be cruel to ourselves when Christ is so gracious.

There is a certain meekness of spirit by which we give thanks to God for any ability at all and rest content with the measure of grace we have received, seeing it is God’s good pleasure that it should be so, who gives both the will and the deed; yet not in such a way that we stop striving further. But when after faithful effort we fall short of what we would like to be, and short of what others are, then let us know for our comfort that Christ will not quench the smoking flax, and that sincerity and truth, as was said before, together with effort to grow, is our perfection. What God says in 1 Kings 14:13 is comforting: He only shall come to the grave in peace, because in him there is found some good thing; only some good thing. Lord, I believe (Mark 9:24): with a weak faith, but with faith. I love You with a faint love, but with love. I strive in a feeble way, but I strive. A little fire is fire, though it smokes. Since You have taken me into Your covenant and made me Yours instead of Your enemy, will You throw me off for these weaknesses, which, as they displease You, are also the grief of my own heart?

fields.title: Resolving the Case of Unwillingness, and Discouragements
fields.body_html:
FROM what has been said, with a little added, it will not be hard to settle the question some need help with: whether we ought to perform our duties when our hearts are completely unwilling. To answer it we must know, 1. Our hearts by themselves hanker after liberty, and are hard to bring under the yoke of duty; and the more spiritual the duty, the more stubborn they are. Corruption gains ground, for the most part, with every neglect. It is like rowing against the tide: one stroke missed will not be made up in three. So it is good to keep our hearts close to duty, and not to listen to the excuses they are ready to invent.

When we set about a duty, God strengthens His own side that He has in us. We find a warmth of heart and an increase of strength, the Spirit going along with us and raising us up by degrees, until He leaves us, as it were, in heaven. God often delights to take advantage of our unwillingness, so that He may show His work more clearly, and so that all the glory of the work may be His, whose strength it all is.

Obedience is most pure when there is nothing else to sweeten the action. Although the sacrifice is imperfect, the obedience with which it is offered is accepted.

What is won as plunder from our corruptions will afterwards bring as much comfort as it now brings trouble. Feeling and freedom of spirit are often held back until the duty is done: reward follows work. In and after duty we find that experience of God’s presence which, without obedience, we may wait for a long time and still go without. This does not limit the Spirit’s freedom to blow upon our souls when He pleases (John 3:8). For we are speaking only of a state of soul that is becalmed, and must row, as it were, against the stream. As in sailing the hand must be on the helm and the eye on the star, so here we must put what little strength we have into our duty, and look up for help, which the Spirit will give as freely as He gives it seasonably.

Yet in those duties that need the body as well as the soul, there may be a pause until strength is restored: sharpening the blade does not hinder the work but fits us for it. 2. In sudden passions there should be time to compose and calm the soul, and to put the strings in tune: the prophet wanted a musician to bring his soul into the right frame. In the same way we are prone to be discouraged in suffering because of our impatience: “Alas, I shall never get through such a cross!” But if God brings us into the cross, He will be with us in the cross, and at length bring us out more refined; we shall lose nothing but dross (Zech. 13:9). In our own strength we cannot bear the least trouble, and with the Spirit’s help we can bear the greatest. The Spirit will put His shoulder under ours to help us bear our weaknesses. The Lord will put His hand under us to lift us up (Psalm 37:24). “Ye have heard of the patience of Job,” says James (5:11). We have heard of his impatience too, but it pleased God mercifully to overlook that. This also gives us comfort in lonely conditions, such as contagious sickness and the like, where we are more directly under God’s hand. Then Christ has a throne of mercy at our bedside, and numbers our tears and our groans. And, to come to the matter we are now dealing with, the sacrament was ordained not for angels but for men; and not for perfect men but for weak men; and not for Christ, who is truth itself, to bind Him, but because our guilty and unbelieving hearts are ready to call truth itself into question. So it was not enough for His goodness to leave us many precious promises; He also gives us seals to strengthen us. And even if we are not as prepared as we should be, let us pray as Hezekiah did: “The good Lord pardon every one that prepareth his heart to seek God, the Lord God of his fathers, though he be not cleansed according to the purification of the sanctuary” (2 Chron. 30:18–19). Then we come to this holy sacrament with comfort and with much fruit. This should carry us through every duty with great cheerfulness: if we hate our corruptions and strive against them, they will not be counted as ours. “It is no more I,” says Saint Paul, “but sin that dwelleth in me” (Rom. 7:17). For what displeases us will never hurt us, and God will regard us as what we love, desire and labour to be. What we desire to be, we shall be; and what we truly desire to conquer, we shall conquer; for God “will fulfil the desire of them that fear him” (Psalm 145:19). The desire is a pledge of the thing desired. How little encouragement it takes to carry us into the business of this life! And yet all the helps God offers can hardly overcome our reluctant natures. Where, then, do discouragements come from? 1. Not from the Father, for He has bound Himself by covenant to pity us “as a father pitieth his children” (Psalm 103:13), and to accept our weak efforts as a father does. Whatever is lacking in the strength of our duty, He allows us to make up from His gracious kindness, and by this we honour the grace He delights in as much as we would by more perfect performances.

2. Not from Christ, for by His very office He will not quench the smoking flax. We see how Christ gives the best fruits of His love to people who are lowly in station, weak in ability, and offensive in their weaknesses, even in grosser falls. First, it pleases Him in this way to confound the pride of the flesh, which usually measures God’s love by some outward excellence. Secondly, He delights in this way to show the freedom of His grace and His royal prerogative, so that “he that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord.”

In the eleventh chapter of Hebrews, among that cloud of witnesses, we see Rahab, Gideon and Samson ranked with Abraham, the father of the faithful (Heb. 11:31–32). Our blessed Saviour, as He was the image of His Father, was of the same mind in this, glorifying His Father for revealing the mystery of the gospel to simple men and passing over those who had the greatest reputation for wisdom in the world.

It is worth remembering what Saint Augustine tells of a simple man in his time, almost entirely without the use of reason. He was the most patient of men under any injury done to himself, yet out of reverence for religion he would not endure any injury done to the name of Christ. He would even throw stones at those who blasphemed, and in that cause would not spare his own masters. This shows that no one’s abilities are so low that they are beneath the gracious regard of Christ. Where it pleases Him to make His choice and to exalt His mercy, He passes over no level of understanding, however plain.

3. Nor do discouragements come from the Spirit. He helps our weaknesses, and by His office is a Comforter (Rom. 8:26). If He convicts us of sin and so humbles us, it is to make way for His work of comforting us. Discouragements, then, must come from ourselves and from Satan, who works to fasten on us a loathing of duty.

fields.title: Weaknesses Are No Cause for Discouragement: In Whom They Are, and How to Recover Lost Peace
fields.body_html:
AMONG the other causes of discouragement, some are much troubled with scruples, even about the best duties. This comes partly from bodily disorder, helped by Satan’s malice, who throws dust in their eyes on their way to heaven; and partly from some remaining ignorance, which, like darkness, breeds fears. It comes from ignorance of other things, but especially of this merciful disposition in Christ, and being persuaded of it would easily banish false fears. They picture Him as one lying in wait to seize every advantage against them, and in this they may see how they wrong not only themselves but His goodness. This scrupulousness is, for the most part, a sign of a godly soul, as some weeds are a sign of good soil. So such people are all the more to be pitied, for it is a heavy affliction, and in most of them it springs not so much from trouble of conscience as from a sickness of the imagination. The purpose of Christ’s coming was to free us from all such groundless fears.

There is still in some such ignorance of the comforting condition we are in under the covenant of grace that they are greatly discouraged by it. So we must know, 1. that weaknesses do not break our covenant with God. They do not break it between husband and wife; and shall we make ourselves more compassionate than Christ, who makes Himself a pattern of love to all other husbands?

2. Weaknesses do not shut us out from mercy; rather, they incline God to us all the more. Mercy is part of the Church’s marriage settlement: Christ marries her in mercy (Psalm 78:39). The husband is bound to bear with the wife as the weaker vessel (Hos. 2:19); and shall we think He will exempt Himself from His own rule, and not bear with His weak bride?

3. If Christ were not merciful to our weaknesses, He would have no people to serve Him.

Suppose, then, that we are very weak. Still, as long as we are not found among malicious opponents and underminers of God’s truth, let us not give way to despairing thoughts: we have a merciful Saviour. But so that we do not flatter ourselves without grounds, we must know that weaknesses are counted as either, 1. imperfections clinging to our best actions; or, 2. actions that come from being young in Christ, while we are babes; or, 3. from lack of strength, where there has been little teaching; or, 4. sudden, unconsidered outbursts, contrary to our general bent and purpose, while our judgment is clouded by a sudden temptation. Afterwards, 1. we are aware of our weakness; 2. we grieve over it; 3. out of grief we complain; and 4. while complaining we strive and labour to reform, and in labouring we gain some ground on our corruption.

Weaknesses seen in this way, though they are a reason for humility and the object of our daily putting to death of sin, may still stand alongside boldness with God. A good work is neither put out by them nor so tainted that it loses all acceptance with God. But to make excuses for a weakness is more than a weakness; to permit ourselves our weaknesses is more than weakness. Justifying evil seals up the lips, so that the soul cannot call God Father with that childlike freedom, or enjoy sweet fellowship with Him, until peace is made by shaming ourselves and renewing our faith. Those who have ever been bruised for sin recover quickly if they fall. Peter was restored by one gracious look from Christ; David by Abigail’s words. Tell a thief or a vagrant that he is off the road, and he does not care, because his aim is not to walk in any certain road, but only as it suits his own purposes. To make this clearer, we must understand, 1. that wherever there are sins of weakness, the life of grace must have begun in that person. There can be no weakness where there is no life. 2. There must be a sincere and general bent toward the best things. Though a godly man may suddenly be drawn or driven aside in some particulars, yet because of the claim the Spirit of Christ has on him, and because his aims are right in the main, he will either recover by himself or yield to the counsel of others. 3. There must be a right judgment that approves the best ways. Otherwise the heart is rotten and pours corruption into the whole of life, so that every action is infected at the source. Such people justify looseness and condemn God’s ways as too strict; the principles they act on are not good. 4. There must be a married love for Christ, so that on no terms will they change their Lord and husband and give themselves over completely to be ruled by their own lusts or the lusts of others.

A Christian’s behaviour toward Christ may in many things be very offensive, and cause some coolness between them. Yet he will own Christ, and Christ will own him. He will not settle on any course in which he knows he must break with Christ.

Where the heart is qualified like this in these respects, we must know that Christ counts it His honour to pass over many weaknesses; indeed, in weaknesses He makes His strength perfect. There are some almost unconquerable weaknesses, such as forgetfulness, heaviness of spirit, sudden passions, fears and so on, which, though natural, are for the most part tainted with sin. If the life of Christ is in us, we are weary of these and would gladly shake them off, as a sick man would his fever. Otherwise it should be counted not so much weakness as wilfulness; and the more will there is, the more sin there is. And little sins, when God awakens the conscience and sets them in order before us (Ps. 50:21), will prove great burdens, and will not only bruise a reed but shake a cedar. Yet God’s children never sin with their full will, because there is a contrary law of the mind, by which the rule of sin is broken, and which is always working secretly against the law of sin. Even so, there may be so much will in a sinful action that it badly wastes our comfort afterwards, and keeps us a long time on the rack of a troubled conscience, God in His fatherly dealings holding back the sense of His love. As far as we give way to our will in sinning, so far do we set ourselves at a distance from comfort. Sin against conscience is like a flaw in a candlewick, which wastes our joy and so weakens our strength. We must know, then, that deliberate breaches in holiness will greatly hinder the sense of our justification.

What course should such people take to recover their peace?

They must pass a sharp sentence on themselves, and yet throw themselves on God’s mercy in Christ, as they did at their first conversion. And now they need to cling to Christ all the more tightly, as they see more need in themselves. Let them remember the gentleness of Christ here, who will not quench the smoking flax. We often see that after a deep humbling, Christ speaks more peace than before, to bear witness to the truth of the reconciliation. He does this because He knows Satan’s schemes to cast such people down lower, and because such people are most humbled in themselves and are ashamed to look Christ in the face because of their unkindness. We see that God not only pardoned David, but after much bruising gave him wise Solomon to succeed him on the throne. We see in the Song of Songs (6:4) that after the Church had been humbled for slighting Christ, Christ sweetly welcomes her again and begins to praise her beauty. We must know, for our comfort, that Christ was not anointed to this great work of Mediator for lesser sins only, but for the greatest, if we have only a spark of true faith to take hold of Him. So if there is any bruised reed, let him not exclude himself when Christ does not exclude him: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden” (Matt. 11:28). Why should we not make use of so gracious a disposition? We are poor only because we do not know our riches in Christ. In time of temptation, believe Christ rather than the devil. Believe truth from Truth itself. Do not listen to a liar, an enemy and a murderer.

fields.title: Satan Is Not to Be Believed in How He Pictures Christ to Us
fields.body_html:
SINCE Christ is set before us in so comforting a light, let us not believe Satan’s portraits of Him. When we are troubled in conscience over our sins, his way is to present Christ to the afflicted soul as a most severe judge, armed with justice against us. But then let us present Him to our souls as God Himself has set Him before our eyes: holding out a sceptre of mercy and spreading His arms to receive us. When we think of Joseph, Daniel, John the Evangelist and others, we picture them with delight as gentle and sweet people. How much more, when we think of Christ, should we picture Him as a mirror of all meekness! If the sweetness of all flowers were in one, how sweet that flower must be! In Christ all the perfections of mercy and love meet; how great, then, must be the mercy that lives in so gracious a heart! Whatever tenderness is scattered among husbands, fathers, brothers and heads is only a beam from Him; it is in Him in the highest degree. We are weak, but we are His; we are disfigured, but we still bear His image. A father does not look so much at his child’s blemishes as at his own nature in him. So Christ finds reason to love in what is His own in us. He sees His own nature in us. We are diseased, but we are still His members. Who ever neglected his own members because they were sick or weak? No one ever hated his own flesh. Can the head forget the members? Can Christ forget Himself? We are His fullness as He is ours. He was love itself clothed in human nature, which He joined so closely to Himself so that He might share His goodness with us more freely. And He took our nature not when it was at its best, but when it was brought low, with all the natural and common weaknesses it was subject to. So let us loathe all suspicious thoughts, as either thrown in or nursed by that damned spirit. As he worked to divide the Father and the Son by stirring up doubts (“If thou be the Son of God,” Matt. 4:6), so his daily study is to divide the Son and us, by breeding false beliefs in us about Christ, as if there were no such tender love in Him for people like us. It was his craft from the beginning to discredit God with man by calling God’s love into question, as he did with our first father Adam. His success then keeps him ready with that weapon still.

“But for all this,” says the smoking flax, “I do not feel Christ to be like this toward me, but quite the opposite. He seems to be my enemy. I see and feel evidence of His just displeasure.”

Christ may play the part of an enemy for a little while, as Joseph did, but it is to make way for playing His own part of mercy at a better time. He cannot hold back His compassion for long. He seems to wrestle with us, as with Jacob, but He supplies us with hidden strength to win in the end. Faith pulls the mask off His face and sees a loving heart under appearances to the contrary. At first He answers the woman of Canaan, crying after Him, not a word. 2. Then He refuses her. 3. Then He gives an answer that seems to shame her, calling her a dog, as one outside the covenant. Yet she would not be beaten off like that, for she considered the purpose of His coming. As His Father was never nearer Him in strength to support Him than when He was furthest away in any sense of favour to comfort Him, so Christ is never nearer us in power to uphold us than when He seems most to hide His presence from us. The influence of the Sun of Righteousness goes deeper than His light. In such cases, whatever Christ’s present behaviour toward us may be, let us set His nature and office against it. He cannot deny Himself; He cannot fail to carry out the office His Father has laid on Him. We see here that the Father has undertaken that He will not quench the smoking flax; and Christ in turn undertakes for us to the Father, appearing before Him for us until He presents us blameless before Him (John 17:6, 11). The Father has given us to Christ, and Christ gives us back again to the Father.

“This would be good comfort, if only I were even smoking flax.”

Answer. It is good that your objection pinches yourself and not Christ; it is good that you give Him the honour of His mercy toward others, though not toward yourself. But still, do not wrong the work of His Spirit in your heart. As Satan slanders Christ to us, so he slanders us to ourselves. If you are not even smoking flax, then why do you not renounce your share in Christ and disown the covenant of grace? You dare not do this. Why do you not give yourself up wholly to other satisfactions? Your spirit will not let you. Where do these restless groans and complaints come from? Lay your present condition alongside this office of Christ toward such people, and do not despise the consolation of the Almighty, or refuse your own mercy. Throw yourself into the arms of Christ, and if you perish, perish there. If you do not, you are sure to perish. If mercy is to be found anywhere, it is there. Christ’s care for you shows in this: He has given you a heart that is in some degree sensitive. He might have given you up to hardness, complacency and a profane heart, the greatest of all spiritual judgments. He who died for His enemies, will He refuse those whose souls long for Him? He who by His messengers urges us to be reconciled, will He put us off when we earnestly seek it from His hand? No, without doubt, when He goes ahead of us by kindling holy desires in us, He is ready to meet us in His own ways. When the prodigal set out to return to his father, his father did not wait for him but met him on the way. When He prepares the heart to seek, He will cause His ear to hear (Psalm 10:17). He cannot bring Himself to hide from us for long. If God should bring us into so dark a condition that we see no light from Himself or from any creature, then let us remember what He says by the prophet Isaiah: “Who is among you that... walketh in darkness, and hath no light” (Isaiah 50:10), no light of comfort, no light of God’s face? “Let him trust in the name of the Lord.” We can never be in a condition where there is just cause for utter despair. So let us do as sailors do, and cast anchor in the dark. Christ knows how to pity us in this case. Whatever comfort He felt from His Father in His breaking (Isaiah 53:5), we shall feel the same from Him in our bruising.

The sighs of a bruised heart carry in them some report, both of our love for Christ and of His care for us. The eyes of our souls cannot turn toward Him unless He has first cast a gracious look on us. The least love we have for Him is only a reflection of His love shining on us first. As Christ did in His own example everything He commands us to do, so He suffered in His own person everything He calls us to suffer, so that He might the better learn to relieve and pity us in our sufferings. In His desertion in the garden and on the cross, He was willing to go without the unspeakable comfort of His Father’s presence, both to bear the wrath of the Lord for a time on our behalf and also to know better how to comfort us in our greatest extremities. God sees fit that we should taste a little of the cup His Son drank so deeply, so that we might feel a little of what sin is and what His Son’s love was. But our comfort is that Christ drank the dregs of the cup for us, and will help us, so that our spirits do not utterly fail under the little taste of His displeasure we may feel. He became not only a man but a curse, a man of sorrows, for us. He was broken so that we would not be broken; He was troubled so that we would not be troubled to despair; He became a curse so that we would not be cursed. Whatever could be wished for in an all-sufficient comforter is all found in Christ. 1. Authority: all power was given Him by the Father. 2. Strength in Himself, as His name is the Mighty God (Isaiah 9:6). 3. Wisdom, knowing from His own experience how and when to help. 4. Willingness, as being flesh of our flesh and bone of our bone.

fields.title: A Rebuke to Those Who Sin against Christ’s Merciful Disposition; on Quenching the Spirit
fields.body_html:
WE must now take notice of several kinds of people who offend deeply against this merciful disposition of Christ. 1. Those who go on in every evil course of life with the notion that it would be useless to go to Christ, their lives have been so bad. Yet as soon as we look toward heaven, every encouragement is ready to meet us and draw us forward. Among others, this is one attraction: that Christ is ready to welcome us and lead us further. No one in the church is damned except those who choose to be. And there are those who force hard thoughts of Christ on themselves, so that they may have some show of reason for seeking contentment in other things, like that unprofitable servant (Matt. 25:30) who insisted on believing that his master was a hard man, and so flattered himself in his unfruitful ways and in not using the talent he had. 2. Those who invent a hope of their own that Christ will let them walk in the ways to hell and still bring them to heaven. But all comfort should draw us nearer to Christ; otherwise it is a lying comfort, either in itself or in the way we apply it. And 3. Those who throw water themselves on the sparks Christ is working to kindle in them, because they do not want to be troubled by their light. Such people must know that the Lamb can be angry, and that those who will not come under His sceptre of mercy will be broken in pieces by His sceptre of power (Psalm 2:9). Though He will graciously tend and keep alive the smallest spark of true grace, yet where He finds no spark of grace, but only resistance to His Spirit striving with them, His wrath once kindled will burn to hell. There is no more just provocation than kindness rudely refused. When God would have healed Babylon and she would not be healed, she was given up to destruction (Jer. 51:9). When Jerusalem would not be gathered under Christ’s wing, her house was left desolate (Matt. 23:37–38). When Wisdom stretches out her hand and people refuse, Wisdom will laugh at their destruction (Prov. 1:26). Salvation itself will not save those who spill the medicine and throw away the bandage. It is a pitiful case when this merciful Saviour takes delight in destruction, when He who made them will have no mercy on them (Isa. 27:11). “Oh,” say the rebels of our time, “God did not make us to damn us.” Yes, but if you will not meet Christ in the ways of His mercy, it is right that you should eat the fruit of your own way and be filled with your own schemes (Prov. 1:31). This will be the hell of hell: when people realize that they loved their sins more than their souls, and when they think of what love and mercy was all but forced on them, and yet they chose to perish. The more we have a hand in pulling a judgment down on ourselves, the more the conscience will be confounded within itself, when they acknowledge Christ to be wholly without blame and themselves to be without excuse.

If people appeal to their own consciences, these will tell them that the Holy Spirit has often knocked at their hearts, willing to kindle some holy desires in them. How else could they be said to resist the Holy Ghost, unless the Spirit was readier to draw them on to further goodness than their own wills would allow? So those in the Church who are damned have condemned themselves beforehand. Here, then, we need not climb to higher causes, when people carry a sufficient cause in their own hearts.

4. And the best of us may offend against this merciful disposition if we are not on guard against the liberty our fleshly natures are ready to take from it. This is how we reason: “Christ will not quench the smoking flax, so why should we fear that any neglect on our part can bring us into a comfortless condition? If Christ will not do it, what can?”

Answer. You know the apostle’s command, all the same: “Quench not the Spirit” (1 Thess. 5:19). These warnings against quenching are made holy by the Spirit as means of not quenching. Christ fulfils His office of not quenching by stirring up fitting efforts in us; and no one is more careful in using the means than those who are most certain of a good outcome. The reason is this: the means God has set apart for bringing anything about fall under the same purpose He has to bring that thing to pass. This principle is taken for granted even in ordinary affairs. Who, if he knew in advance that it would be a fruitful year, would therefore hang up his plough and neglect his fields? So the apostle stirs us up from the sure expectation of a blessing (1 Cor. 15:57–58), and this encouragement here, from the good outcome of final victory, is meant to stir us up, not to hold us back. If we are careless in exercising the grace we have received and in using the means appointed, letting our spirits be weighed down with the many and various cares of this life, and not guarding against the chill of the times, then for such failings God in His wise care often lets us fall into a worse condition, as far as feeling goes, than those who were never so enlightened. Yet in mercy He will not let us be such enemies to ourselves as to neglect wholly these sparks once kindled. If it were possible for us to be given up to abandoning all effort completely, we could expect no other outcome than quenching. But Christ will tend this spark and nourish this small seed, so that He will always keep some degree of care in the soul. If we want to use this for our comfort, we must consider all the means by which Christ preserves grace once begun. First, holy fellowship, by which one Christian warms another: “Two are better than one” (Eccles. 4:9). “Did not our heart burn within us?” said the disciples (Luke 24:32). Secondly, much fellowship with God in holy duties, such as meditation and prayer, which not only kindles the soul but adds a brightness to it. Thirdly, we find by experience that the breath of the Spirit goes along with the breath of the ministry, which is why the apostle joins these two together: “Quench not the Spirit. Despise not prophesyings” (1 Thess. 5:19–20). Nathan, with a few words, blew the dying sparks in David back into flame. Rather than let His fire in us die, God will send some Nathan or other; and something is always left in us to join with the word as natural to it, as a coal that has fire in it will quickly catch more: smoking flax easily takes fire. Fourthly, grace is strengthened by being used. “Arise therefore, and be doing, and the Lord be with thee,” said David to his son Solomon (1 Chron. 22:16). “Stir up the gift of God, which is in thee,” for in this way holy impulses turn into resolutions, resolutions into practice, and practice into a ready preparedness for every good work. Yet let us know that grace grows by being used, not because of the use itself, but as Christ by His Spirit flows into the soul, draws us nearer to Himself, the fountain, and pours such comfort into the act that the heart is further enlarged. The heart of a Christian is Christ’s garden, and His graces are like so many sweet spices and flowers, which His Spirit blows upon and makes them give off a sweet fragrance. So keep the soul open to welcome the Holy Ghost, for He will continually bring in fresh forces to overcome corruption, and most of all on the Lord’s Day. John was in the Spirit on the Lord’s Day, even on Patmos, the place of his banishment (Rev. 1:10). Then the winds of the Spirit blow more strongly and sweetly. So as we look for the comfort of this teaching, let us not indulge our natural laziness, but train ourselves for godliness (1 Tim. 4:7), and labour to keep this fire always burning on the altar of our hearts, trimming our lamps daily, putting in fresh oil, and winding our souls up higher and higher. To settle down in a good condition is contrary to grace, which cannot help pressing on to a further measure. Let no one turn this grace into lawlessness (Jude 4). Weaknesses are a reason for humility, not an excuse for carelessness, nor an encouragement to presumption. We should be so far from being bad because Christ is good that those coals of love should melt us. So those in whom the thought of Christ’s gentleness does not work this way may well suspect themselves. Surely where grace is, corruption is like smoke to the eyes and vinegar to the teeth (Prov. 10:26). So such people will labour, for the sake of their own comfort as well as for the credit of religion and the glory of God, that their light may break out. If a spark of faith or love is so precious, what an honour it will be to be rich in faith! Who would not rather walk in the light and in the comforts of the Holy Ghost than live in a dark and perplexed state? Who would not rather be carried to heaven under full sail than always be tossed about with fears and doubts? The present trouble of fighting against a sin is not as great as the unrest that any corruption we indulge will bring on us afterwards. True peace is in conquering, not in giving in. The comfort intended in this text is for those who would gladly do better but find their corruptions holding them back; who are in such a fog that they often cannot tell what to think of themselves; who would gladly believe, and yet often fear they do not believe, and think it cannot be that God should be so good to such sinful wretches as they are; and yet who do not indulge themselves in these fears and doubts. And among others, how they wrong themselves and Him, those who will have other mediators to God for them than Him! Is anyone more compassionate than He, who became man for this very purpose, that He might be compassionate to His own flesh? Let us all at all times go to this meek Saviour, and present all our requests in His prevailing name. Why should we knock at any other door? Can anyone be more tender toward us than Christ? What encouragement we have to commend the state of the Church in general, or of any broken-hearted Christian, to Him in our prayers! We may speak of them to Christ as they spoke of Lazarus: “Lord, the Church whom You love, and for whom You gave Yourself, is in distress. Lord, this poor Christian, for whom You were bruised (Isa. 53:5), is bruised and brought very low.” It cannot fail to move His heart when the misery of those so dear to Him is spread before Him.

Again, considering this gracious nature in Christ, let us think to ourselves like this: when He is so kind to us, shall we be cruel against Him, in His name, in His truth, in His children? How can those who delight in being so terrible to the meek of the earth (Zeph. 2:3) hope to look so gracious a Saviour in the face? Those who are so violent toward His bride will learn one day that they were dealing with Him Himself in His Church. And it cannot fail to cut to the heart those who have felt this love of Christ to hear Him wounded who is the life of their lives and the soul of their souls. This makes those who have felt mercy weep over Christ, whom they have pierced with their sins. There cannot fail to be a mutual and lively sympathy between the head and the members. When we are tempted to any sin, even if we will not pity ourselves, we should still spare Christ, and not put Him to new torments. The apostle could find no more heart-breaking argument to urge us to offer ourselves to God than to appeal to us by the mercies of God in Christ.

This mercy of Christ should also move us to feel for the condition of the poor Church, torn by enemies outside and tearing itself apart with divisions at home. It cannot fail to work on any soul that ever felt comfort from Christ to consider how tenderly the apostle pleads for agreement in judgment and in love: “If there be therefore any consolation in Christ, if any comfort of love, if any fellowship of the Spirit, if any bowels and mercies, fulfil ye my joy, that ye be likeminded” (Phil. 2:1–2). It is as if he said, “Unless you will disown all consolation in Christ, labour to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.” What a joyful sight it is for Satan and his side to see those who are separated from the world fall to pieces among themselves! Our discord is our enemy’s music.

All the more to blame, then, are those who for private aims cultivate differences from others, and will not let the wounds of the Church close and heal. This must not be taken to mean that people should hide their judgment on any truth where there is just cause to speak. For the least truth is Christ’s and not ours, so we are not free to affirm or deny as we please. A penny is owed as truly as a pound, so we must be faithful in the least truth. When the time calls for it, our words are like apples of gold in pictures of silver. One word spoken in season will do more good than a thousand out of season. But in some cases peace, kept by holding our faith to ourselves (Rom. 14:22), matters more than openly declaring some things we believe to be true. For human nature is so weak that any difference of opinion can hardly be brought into the open without some cooling of affection. As far as people are not of one mind, they will hardly be of one heart, except where grace and the peace of God (Col. 3:15) rule strongly in the heart. So an open show of difference is never good except when it is necessary. Some, out of a desire to be somebody, turn into side paths and give in to a spirit of contradiction in themselves; yet if Saint Paul may be the judge, are they not carnal (1 Cor. 3:3)? If it is wisdom, it is wisdom from below; for the wisdom from above is pure and also peaceable (James 3:17). When our blessed Saviour was about to leave the world, what did He press on His disciples more than peace and love? And in His last prayer, how earnestly He begged His Father that they might be one, as He and the Father were one (John 17:21)! But what He prayed for on earth we shall enjoy perfectly only in heaven. Let this make thinking about that time all the sweeter to us.

And to expose further those who offend in this way: what spirit shall we think they are of, who take advantage of the bruised state and weaknesses of people’s spirits to soothe them with false peace for their own worldly ends? A wounded spirit will part with anything. Most of the profitable doctrines of the papal system, such as confession, satisfaction, merit, purgatory and the like, spring from this. But they are physicians of no value, or rather tormentors than physicians at all. Being delivered from the sting of these scorpions is a greater blessing than we are thankful for. Spiritual tyranny is the greatest tyranny, and especially so where most mercy should be shown. Yet even there some, like cruel surgeons, delight in making cures last a long time, to profit themselves from the misery of others. It brings people under a terrible curse when they do not remember to show mercy, but persecute the poor and needy man, so that they might even kill the broken in heart (Psalm 109:16).

The same goes for those who gain worldly advantage from the spiritual misery of others. Add to them those who build up estates by betraying the Church, and are unfaithful in the trust given to them, when the children cry for the bread of life and there is no one to give it to them. In this way they bring on the people of God that heavy judgment of a spiritual famine, starving Christ in His members. Shall we repay so good a Saviour like this, who counts the love and mercy shown in feeding His lambs (John 21:15) as shown to Himself?

Last of all, those behave very unkindly toward Christ who stumble at His stooping so low to us in His government and ordinances, who are ashamed of the simplicity of the gospel, who count preaching foolishness.

Out of the pride of their hearts, they think they can do well enough without the help of the word and sacraments. They think Christ did not put on enough grandeur, and so they will improve matters with inventions of their own, by which they can better please flesh and blood, as in the papal system. What greater ingratitude can there be than to despise any help Christ in mercy has provided for us? In the days of His flesh, the proud Pharisees took offence at His familiar dealings with sinners, though He did this only as a physician, to heal their souls. What defences Saint Paul was driven to make for himself because of his plainness in setting out the gospel! The further Christ, in Himself and in His servants, comes down to lift us up, the more we should welcome that love with all humility and readiness, and praise the goodness of God who has put the great work of our salvation, and laid the government, on so gentle a Saviour, one who will behave so gently in everything in which He deals between God and us, and between us and God. The lower Christ comes down to us, the higher let us lift Him up in our hearts. All those who have ever experienced Christ’s work in their hearts will do this.

fields.title: Christ’s Judgment in Us, and His Victory: What It Is
fields.body_html:
WE come to the third part: the steady advance of Christ’s gracious power, until He has set up so complete a government in us that it prevails over all corruptions. It is said here that He will nourish His beginnings of grace in us until He brings forth judgment unto victory. By judgment here is meant the kingdom of grace in us, that government by which Christ sets up a throne in our hearts. Rulers among the Jews were first called judges, then kings, and so this inward rule is called judgment. It is also called so because it agrees with the judgment of the word, which the psalmist often calls judgment (Psalm 72:1–2), because it agrees with God’s judgment. People may read their sentence in God’s word: what it judges of them, God judges of them. By this judgment set up in us, good is discerned, approved and done; sin is judged, condemned and put to death. Our spirit, being under the Spirit of Christ, is governed by Him; and as far as it is governed by Christ, it governs us graciously.

Christ and we are of one judgment and one will. He has His will in us, and His judgments are so planted in us that they become our own judgment, as we carry His law in our hearts, written by His Spirit (Jer. 31:33). The law in the inner man and the written law answer each other like the two halves of a matching deed.

The meaning, then, is that the gracious structure of holiness set up in our hearts by the Spirit of Christ will go forward until every opposing power is brought under. The spirit of judgment will be a spirit of burning (Isaiah 4:4), to consume whatever opposing corruption eats into the soul like rust. If God’s builders fall into errors and build stubble on a good foundation, God’s Spirit, like a spiritual fire, will in time reveal this (1 Cor. 3:13) and burn it up. By a spirit of judgment they will condemn their own errors and ways. The whole work of grace in us is described under the name of judgment, and sometimes of wisdom, because judgment is the chief and leading part of grace. That is why the gracious work of repentance is called a change of mind, a wisdom that comes afterwards. On the other hand, in the learned languages the words that express wisdom also suggest the general relish and taste of the whole soul, and the judgment of taste rather than of sight or any other sense, because taste is the most necessary sense, and needs the object brought nearer than any other. So in the spiritual life it is most necessary that the Spirit should change the taste of the soul, so that it savours the things of the Spirit so deeply that all other things lose their flavour. And as it is true of every individual Christian that Christ’s judgment in him will be victorious, so it is true of the whole body of Christians, the Church. The government of Christ, and His truth, by which He rules as with a sceptre, will at length be victorious in spite of Satan, Antichrist and every enemy. Christ, riding on His white horse (Rev. 6:2), has a bow, and goes out conquering (Rev. 19:11) in the ministry, so that He may overcome either to conversion or to ruin. But still I take judgment here chiefly for Christ’s kingdom and government within us. 1. Because God especially requires the submission of the soul and conscience as His own throne. 2. Because if judgment prevailed in everything around us and not in our own hearts, it would bring us no comfort. That is why it is the first thing we desire when we pray, “Thy kingdom come”: that Christ would come and rule in our hearts. The kingdom of Christ in His ordinances serves only to bring Christ home to His own place, our hearts.

The words being explained in this way, so that judgment here includes the government of mind, will and affections, several conclusions naturally spring from them.

fields.title: Christ Is Gentle, Yet He Will Govern Those Who Enjoy the Comfort of His Gentleness
fields.body_html:
THE first conclusion, from the way this part of the verse is joined to the one before it, is that Christ is gentle on these terms: He will set up His government in those He is so gentle and tender toward. He pardons in such a way that He will be obeyed as a king. He takes us to be His bride in such a way that He will be obeyed as a husband. The same Spirit who convinces us that we need His righteousness to cover us also convinces us that we need His government to rule us. His love for us moves Him to shape us to be like Himself, and our love for Him stirs us up to be people He can delight in. Nor do we have any more faith or hope than we have care to be purified as He is pure. He makes us governors under Him, indeed kings under Himself, giving us grace not only to resist but in some measure to overcome our base desires. One chief fruit of Christ’s exaltation is that He may turn every one of us from our wickedness (Acts 3:26). For this purpose Christ died, rose again and lives, that He might be Lord of both the dead and the living (Rom. 14:9). God has bound Himself by an oath to grant us that we might serve Him without fear, in holiness and righteousness in His sight (Luke 1:74–75), and not only in the sight of the world. 1. This may serve as a test to discern who may rightly claim Christ’s mercy: only those who will take His yoke, and count it a greater happiness to be under His government than to enjoy any liberty of the flesh; who will take the whole Christ, and not pick out of Him only what suits their present comfort; who will not divide Lord from Jesus and so make a Christ of their own. No one ever truly desired pardoning mercy without also desiring healing mercy. David prays for a new spirit as well as for a sense of pardoning mercy (Psalm 51).

2. This shows that those are mistaken who make Christ only our righteousness, and our sanctification only by imputation. For it is a great part of our happiness to be under such a Lord, who was not only born for us and given to us, but also has the government on His shoulders (Isa. 9:6–7). He is our sanctifier as well as our Saviour; our Saviour from the power of sin by the effective power of His Spirit, as well as from its guilt by the merit of His death. So let this be remembered: 1. The first and chief ground of our comfort is that Christ, as a priest, offered Himself as a sacrifice to His Father for us. The guilty soul flees first to Christ crucified, made a curse for us. From this Christ has the right to govern us; from this He gives us His Spirit as our guide to lead us home.

2. In the course of our life, after we are in a state of grace, if we are overtaken by any sin, we must remember to go first to Christ’s mercy to pardon us, and then to the promise of His Spirit to govern us.

3. And when we feel ourselves cold in love and duty, the best way is to warm ourselves at this fire of His love and mercy in giving Himself for us.

4. Again, remember this: as Christ rules us, He does it by a spirit of love that comes from a sense of His love, which makes His commandments easy for us. He leads us by His free Spirit, a spirit of liberty. His subjects are volunteers. The only compulsion He lays on His subjects is that of love; He draws us sweetly with the cords of love. Yet remember also that He draws us strongly by a spirit of power. For it is not enough that we have reasons and encouragements to love and obey Christ from that love of His by which He gave Himself to justify us. Christ’s Spirit must also overcome our hearts and make them holy to love Him; without that, all reasons would be useless. Our disposition must be changed; we must be new creatures. Those who look for spiritual love in an unchanged heart are looking for heaven in hell. When a child obeys his father, he does so both because reasons persuade him and because of a childlike nature that gives those reasons their strength. It is natural for a child of God to love Christ as far as he is renewed, not only because reason persuades him to, but also from an inward principle and work of grace, which gives those reasons their main force. First we are made partakers of the divine nature, and then we are easily persuaded and led by Christ’s Spirit to spiritual duties.

fields.title: The Spiritual Government of Christ Is Joined with Judgment and Wisdom
fields.body_html:
THE second conclusion is that Christ’s government in His Church and in His children is a wise and well-ordered government, because it is called judgment, and judgment is the life and soul of wisdom. This conclusion has two branches: 1. that the spiritual government of Christ in us is joined with judgment and wisdom; 2. that wherever there is true spiritual wisdom and judgment, the Spirit of Christ also brings in His gracious government. As for the first, a life well guided by the rules of Christ agrees with the strongest and highest reason of all. That is why holy people are called the children of wisdom (Luke 7:35), and are able to justify all the ways of wisdom by both reason and experience. Opposite ways are folly and madness. That is why Saint Paul says that a spiritual man judges all things (1 Cor. 2:15) that concern him, and is judged by no one of a lower rank, because they lack the spiritual light and sight to judge. Yet people of this kind will insist on judging, and speak evil of what they do not understand (2 Pet. 2:12). They step from ignorance to prejudice and rash condemnation without passing through right judgment on the way, and so their judgment comes to nothing. But the judgment of a spiritual man, as far as he is spiritual, will stand, because it agrees with the nature of things: as things are in themselves, so they are in his judgment. As God is in Himself infinite in goodness and majesty, so He is to him; in his heart he ascribes to God His divinity and all His excellencies. As Christ is in Himself the only Mediator, and all in all in the Church (Col. 3:11), so He is to him, because he makes Christ so in his heart. As all things are dung compared with Christ (Phil. 3:8), so they are to Paul, a sanctified man. As the very worst thing in religion, the reproach of Christ, is better than the pleasures of sin for a season (Heb. 11:25–26), so it is to Moses, a man of right values. As one day in the courts of God is better than a thousand elsewhere (Ps. 84:10), so it is to David, a man of reformed judgment. A good man’s judgment conforms to things as they are in themselves; as God has made things differ or agree, so his judgment differs or agrees.

Truth is truth, error is error, and what is unlawful is unlawful, whether people think so or not. God has put an eternal difference between light and darkness, good and evil, which no creature’s opinion can change. So no one’s judgment is the measure of things except as far as it agrees with the truth God has stamped on the things themselves. Because a wise man’s judgment agrees with the truth of things, a wise man may in some sense be called the measure of things, and the judgment of one holy, wise man is to be preferred to that of a thousand others. Such people are usually as immovable as the sun in its course, because they think, speak and live by rule. Joshua and his house will serve the Lord (Josh. 24:15), whatever others do, and will run a course contrary to the world, because their judgment leads them the opposite way. That is why Satan has a grudge against the eye of the soul, the judgment, and tries to put it out by ignorance and false reasoning. For he cannot rule in anyone until he has either taken away or perverted the judgment. He is a prince of darkness, and rules in the darkness of the understanding. So he must first be thrown out of the understanding by truth prevailing and being planted in the soul. Those who are enemies of knowledge, then, help Satan and Antichrist, whose kingdom, like Satan’s, is a kingdom of darkness, to set up their throne. That is why Christ promises that the Holy Ghost will convince the world of judgment (John 16:8). That is, He is determined to set up a throne of government, because the great lord of misrule, Satan, the prince of this world, is judged by the gospel and the Spirit who goes with it. His deceptions are uncovered and his schemes laid bare. So when the gospel spread, the oracles fell silent, Satan fell from heaven like lightning (Luke 10:18), and people were transferred out of his kingdom into Christ’s (Col. 1:13). Where victory is won by lies, exposure is victory. “They shall proceed no further: for their folly shall be manifest unto all men” (2 Tim. 3:9). So exposing error stops it, for no one is willingly deceived. Let truth have full scope without check or restraint, and let Satan and his instruments do their worst; they will not prevail. As Jerome said of the Pelagians in his time: “Exposing your opinions is defeating them; your blasphemies show themselves at first sight.”

From this we learn how necessary it is that the understanding be grounded in supernatural knowledge, for the right ordering of a Christian life.

There must be light to reveal a further end than nature, the end for which we are Christians, and a fitting rule directing us to that end. That rule is the will of God in Christ, revealing His good pleasure toward us and our duty toward Him; and by virtue of this revelation we do everything we do that may in any way help our final account. The eye must first be single, and then the whole body and frame of our life will be full of light (Matt. 6:22). Otherwise both we and our way of life are nothing but darkness. The whole life of a Christian is nothing but knowledge digested into will, affection and practice. If the first digestion in the stomach is not good, that in the liver cannot be good. In the same way, if there is error in the judgment, it spoils the whole practice, as an error in the foundation spoils the building. God will have no blind sacrifices and no unreasonable service (Mal. 1:13), but will have us love Him with all our mind (Rom.

12:1), that is, with the understanding part, as well as with all our heart (Luke 10:27), that is, the feeling part of the soul.

This way of Christ governing by judgment suits the soul, and God delights to keep the way of working that is peculiar to man, that is, to do what he does from judgment. As grace presupposes nature and is built on it, so the structure of grace preserves the structure of nature in man. So Christ brings all the good in the soul through the judgment, and does it so sweetly that many, in a dangerous error, think that the good which is in them and comes from them is their own, and not from the powerful work of grace. In the same way, in evil, the devil leads us so subtly along the stream of our own nature that people think Satan had no hand in their sin. But here the mistake carries little danger, because we are evil of ourselves, and the devil only encourages the evil he finds in us. But there are no seeds of supernatural goodness in us at all. God finds nothing in us but hostility. He has only engraved this in our nature: a general inclination toward what we judge to be good. Now when He clearly reveals what is good in particular, we are carried toward it; and when He convincingly reveals what is evil, we loathe it as freely as we embraced it before.

From this we may know whether or not we are working as we should: that is, when we do what we do from inward principles. We should not take up what is good only because we were brought up that way, or because certain people we respect do so, or because we want to stand by a side, so making religion a faction. Rather we should act from judgment: whatever good we do, we first judge in ourselves to be good, and whatever evil we refrain from, we first judge to be evil by an inward judgment. A sound Christian, as he enjoys the better part, has first chosen it, like Mary (Luke 10:42), and he settles all his thoughts by counsel. God does indeed use carnal people for very good service, but without thoroughly changing and convincing their judgment. He works by them, but not in them. So they neither approve the good they do nor hate the evil they refrain from.

fields.title: Where True Wisdom and Judgment Are, There Christ Sets Up His Government
fields.body_html:
THE second branch is that wherever there is true wisdom and judgment, Christ has set up His government. For where wisdom is, it directs us not only to understand but to order our ways rightly. Where Christ by His Spirit teaches as a prophet, He also as a king by His Spirit brings the heart into obedience to what is taught. This is the teaching God has promised, when not only the head but the heart itself is taught; when people not only know what they should do, but are taught the very doing of it. They are taught not only that they should love, fear and obey, but they are taught love itself, and fear and obedience itself. Christ sets up His chair in the very heart, changes its structure, and makes His subjects good while He teaches them to be good. Other princes can make good laws, but they cannot write them in their people’s hearts (Jer. 31:33). This is Christ’s prerogative: He pours His own Spirit into His subjects. On Him rests not only the spirit of wisdom and understanding, but also the spirit of the fear of the Lord (Isa. 11:2). The knowledge we have of Him from Himself is a transforming knowledge (2 Cor. 3:18). The same Spirit who enlightens the mind breathes gracious inclinations into the will and affections, and pours strength into the whole person. As a gracious man judges as he should, so he feels and acts as he judges. His life is a commentary on his inner man. There is a sweet harmony between God’s truth, his judgment and his whole way of life. The heart of a Christian is like Jerusalem at its best, a city compact together, where the thrones of judgment are set (Psalm 122:3, 5). Judgment should have a throne in the heart of every Christian. Not that judgment alone will bring about a change. There must be grace to alter the bent and pull of the will before it will let itself be worked on by the understanding. But God has so joined these together that whenever He shines savingly on the understanding, He gives a soft and pliable heart. For without the Spirit of God working on the heart, it will follow its own inclination toward what it loves, whatever the judgment says to the contrary. There is no natural fit between an unsanctified heart and a sanctified judgment. For the unchanged heart will not let the judgment calmly and soberly conclude what is best, just as a sick man, while his fever spoils his taste, would rather please his taste than listen to what the physician says. Judgment has no power over itself where the will is not brought under, for the will and affections bribe it to give sentence in their favour, whenever some profit or pleasure competes with what the judgment thinks good only in general. So for the most part it lies in the power of the heart what the understanding will judge and decide in particular things. Where grace has brought the heart under, unruly passions do not throw such a fog over the understanding that it cannot see what is best in the particular case; and low motives springing from self-love do not change the case and bend the judgment the opposite way. What is good in itself will be good to us, even though it crosses our particular worldly interests.

Understanding this rightly has a bearing on practice, which is why I have explained it more fully. It will teach us the right method of godliness: to begin with judgment, and then to ask God, together with enlightenment, for holy inclinations of our will and affections, so that a perfect government may be set up in our hearts, and our knowledge may be “in all judgment” (Phil. 1:9), that is, with experience and feeling. When the judgment of Christ is set up in our judgments, and from there, by the Spirit of Christ, brought into our hearts, then it is in its proper place and throne. Until then, truth does us no good, but helps to condemn us. The life of a Christian is an ordered life, and peace will be on the one who walks by the rule of the new creature (Gal. 6:16). The one who despises his ways and loves to live as he pleases, seeking every liberty for the flesh, will die (Prov. 19:16). And Saint Paul confirms it: “If ye live after the flesh, ye shall die” (Rom. 8:13).

We learn too that people whose lives are badly governed have no true judgment: no wicked man can be a wise man. And without Christ’s Spirit the soul is in confusion, without beauty and form, as everything was in the chaos before creation. The whole soul is out of joint until it is set again by Him whose office is to restore all things. The lower part of the soul, which should be subject, rules everything, and keeps down what little truth is in the understanding, holding it captive to low desires. And Satan, through corruption, takes every stronghold of the soul, until Christ, who is stronger than he, comes and drives him out, and takes possession of all the powers and parts of soul and body as weapons of righteousness to serve Him. And then, new lords, new laws: Christ, as a new conqueror, changes the fundamental laws of the old Adam and establishes a government of His own.

fields.title: Christ’s Government Is Victorious
fields.body_html:
THE third conclusion is that this government is victorious. The reasons are:

1. Because Christ has first conquered everything in His own person. He is God over all, blessed for ever (Rom. 9:5), and so over sin, death, hell, Satan, the world and the rest. And as He has overcome them in Himself, so He overcomes them in our hearts and consciences. We used to say that conscience makes a man either a king or a wretch, because it is planted in us to judge for God, either for us or against us. Now if natural conscience is so forceful, what will it be when, besides its own light, it has the light of divine truth put into it? It will certainly prevail, either to make us hold up our heads with boldness or to humble us below ourselves. If by grace it submits to Christ’s truth, then it boldly looks past death, hell, judgment and all spiritual enemies, because then Christ sets up His kingdom in the conscience and makes it a kind of paradise.

The sharpest conflict the soul has is between the conscience and God’s justice. Now if the conscience, sprinkled with the blood of Christ, has prevailed over attacks drawn from the justice of God, now satisfied by Christ, it will prevail over every other opposition whatever.

2. The enemies we have to fight are cursed and damned. So if they begin to fall before the Spirit in us, they will fall; if they rise again, it is only to have a greater fall.

3. The Spirit of truth, into whose care Christ has committed His Church, and the truth of the Spirit, which is the sceptre of Christ, last for ever. So the soul born of the immortal seed of the Spirit (1 Pet. 1:23) and of this truth must not only live for ever, but also prevail over everything that opposes it. For both the word and the Spirit are mighty in their working (Heb. 4:12). And if the evil spirit is never idle in those God hands over to him, we cannot think that the Holy Spirit will be idle in those whose leading and government is committed to Him. No; as He lives in them, so He will drive out everything that rises up against Him, until He is all in all.

What is spiritual is eternal. Truth is a beam of Christ’s Spirit, both in itself and as it is grafted into the soul. So it, and the grace it produces, though little, will prevail. A little thing in the hand of a giant will do great things. A little faith strengthened by Christ will work wonders. 4. “Unto every one that hath shall be given” (Matt. 25:29). Victory over any corruption or temptation is a pledge of final victory. As Joshua said when he set his foot on the five kings he had conquered, “Thus shall the Lord do to all your enemies” (Josh. 10:25). Heaven is ours already; we only strive until we have full possession.

5. Christ as king brings a commanding light into the soul, bows the neck, and softens the iron sinew of the inner man. And where He begins to rule, He rules for ever: of His kingdom there is no end (Luke 1:33).

6. The purpose of Christ’s coming was to destroy the works of the devil, both for us and in us. And the purpose of the resurrection was not only to seal to us the assurance of His victory, but also: 1. to bring our souls to life from death in sin; 2. to free our souls from the snares and sorrows of spiritual death that go with the guilt of sin; 3. to raise them up with more comfort, as the sun breaks out more gloriously from a thick cloud; 4. to raise us up stronger from particular slips and failings; 5. to raise us out of all the troubled and dark conditions of this life; and 6. at length to raise our bodies out of the dust. For the same power the Spirit showed in raising Christ, our head, from the sorrows of death and the lowest point of His humiliation, that same power, obtained from God by the death of Christ, God now being appeased by that sacrifice, the Spirit will show in the Church, which is His body, and in every individual member of it. And this power is conveyed by faith. By faith, after being united to Christ in both His states of humiliation and exaltation, we see ourselves not only dead with Christ but risen and seated together with Him in heavenly places (Eph. 2:6). Now when we grasp that we are dead and risen, and so victorious over all our enemies in our head, and grasp that His aim in all this is to conform us to Himself, we are by this faith changed into His likeness (2 Cor. 3:18). So we become conquerors over all our spiritual enemies, as He is, by the power we draw from Him, who is the storehouse of all spiritual strength for all His people. Christ will at length have His purpose in us. Faith rests assured of it, and this assurance is very active, stirring us up to join with Christ in His purposes.

And so too for the Church in general: by Christ it will have its victory. Christ is that little stone cut out of the mountain without hands, which breaks in pieces that splendid image (Dan. 2:35), that is, every opposing government, until it becomes a great mountain and fills the whole earth. So the stone cut out of the mountain at length becomes a mountain itself. Who are you, then, O mountain, who think you can stand against this mountain? Everything will lie flat and level before it. He will bring down all lofty, high-exalted thoughts and lay low the pride of all flesh. When chaff fights the wind, or stubble the fire, when the heel kicks against the goads, when the potsherd strives with the potter, when man strives against God, it is easy to know which side will win. The winds may toss the ship Christ is in, but not overturn it. The waves may dash against the rock, but they only break themselves against it.

If this is so, why are things as they are with the Church of God, and with many a gracious Christian? The victory seems to go to the enemy.

In answer, remember: 1. God’s children usually overcome in their troubles by suffering. Here lambs overcome lions, and doves overcome eagles, by suffering, so that in this they may be like Christ, who conquered most when He suffered most. Together with Christ’s kingdom of patience there was a kingdom of power.

2. This victory comes by degrees. So those are too hasty who want to conquer as soon as they strike the first blow, and to be at the end of their race as soon as they set out. The Israelites were sure of victory on their journey to Canaan, yet they had to fight it out. God would not have us quickly forget what cruel enemies Christ has overcome for us: “Slay them not, lest my people forget,” says the psalmist (Psalm 59:11). So, by experiencing the harm they do us, we may be kept in fear of coming under their power.

3. God often works by contraries. When He means to give victory, He lets us be beaten at first. When He means to comfort, He terrifies first. When He means to justify, He condemns us first. Those He means to make glorious, He humbles first. A Christian conquers even when he is conquered. When he is conquered by some sins, he gains victory over others more dangerous, such as spiritual pride, complacency and the like.

4. Christ’s work, both in the Church and in the hearts of Christians, often goes backward so that it may go forward better. Seed rots in the ground in winter but afterwards comes up better, and the harder the winter, the more flourishing the spring. In the same way we learn to stand by falling, and gain strength by having our weakness exposed. We take deeper root by being shaken, and as torches flame brighter when they are moved, so it pleases Christ, in His freedom, to maintain His government in us in this way. Let us work at exercising our faith in this, so that it matches Christ’s way of dealing with us. When we are beaten, let us believe we shall overcome; when we have fallen, let us believe we shall rise again. Jacob, after receiving a blow that made him limp, still would not stop wrestling (Gen. 32:24) until he had obtained the blessing. So let us never give up, but in our thoughts join the beginning, progress and end together, and then we shall see ourselves in heaven, out of reach of every enemy. Let us be sure that God’s grace, even in this imperfect state, is stronger than man’s free will was in the state of first perfection, because it is now founded in Christ, who, as He is the author, will also be the finisher of our faith (Heb. 12:2). We are under a more gracious covenant.

What some say, that faith which is rooted continues but weak faith may come to nothing, seems to be contradicted by this Scripture. For as the strongest faith may be shaken, so the weakest, where it is true, is so far rooted that it will prevail. Weakness with watchfulness will hold out, when strength with too much confidence fails. Weakness that is acknowledged is the fittest place and subject for God to perfect His strength in, for awareness of our weaknesses drives us out of ourselves to Him in whom our strength lies.

It follows from this that weakness can stand alongside assurance of salvation. The disciples, in spite of all their weaknesses, are told to rejoice that their names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20). Failings in holiness, where there is a fight against them, should not weaken the peace of our justification and the assurance of our salvation. What matters is not so much what evil is in us as what good; not what corruptions we have, but how we feel toward them; not so much what our particular failings are as what the thread and tenor of our lives is. For Christ’s dislike of what is wrong in us does not turn into hatred of our persons, but into the victorious overcoming of all our weaknesses. Some, after a conflict, have marvelled at the goodness of God, that so small and shaky a faith should have held them up in such great battles, when Satan had almost caught them. And it is indeed a wonder how much a little grace will prevail with God for acceptance, and over our enemies for victory, if the heart is upright. Such is the goodness of our sweet Saviour that He still delights to show His strength in our weakness.

First, then, for the great comfort of poor and weak Christians, let them know that a spark from heaven, even when it is kindled under green wood that hisses and smokes, will consume everything at last. Love once kindled is as strong as death; many waters cannot quench it. So it is called a vehement flame, or a flame of God (Song 8:6), kindled in the heart by the Holy Ghost. The little that is in us is fed by an everlasting spring. As the fire that came down from heaven in Elijah’s time (1 Kings 18:38) licked up all the water, to show that it came from God, so this fire will burn up all our corruptions. No affliction without and no corruption within will quench it. In the morning we often see clouds gather around the sun as if they would hide it, but the sun burns them away little by little until it comes to its full strength. At first, fears and doubts keep this fire from breaking out, until at length it rises above them all and Christ prevails; and then He backs up His own graces in us. Grace conquers us first, and by it we conquer everything else, whether corruptions within us or temptations outside us.

The Church of Christ, born of the word of truth, has the teaching of the apostles for her crown, and tramples the moon, that is, the world and all worldly things, under her feet (Rev. 12:1). “Whatsoever is born of God overcometh the world” (1 John 5:4). Faith, by which above all Christ rules, sets the soul so high that it looks down on everything else as far beneath it, because the Spirit of Christ has shown it riches, honour, beauty and pleasures of a higher kind.
