Now so that we do not fall short of the comfort intended, there are two things especially for us to take note of: 1. whether such a judgment or government, to which this promise of victory is made, is set up in us; 2. some rules or directions for how we should conduct ourselves so that the judgment of Christ in us may indeed be victorious.

The evidences by which we may know that Christ’s judgment in us is the kind that will be victorious are these. 1. If we are able from experience to justify all Christ’s ways, whatever flesh and blood may say to the contrary; if we can willingly agree to the course God has taken in Christ to bring us to heaven; and if we still approve of a further measure of grace than we have reached, and plan and look ahead for it. No other people can justify their ways when their conscience is awakened. 2. When the reasons of religion are the strongest reasons for us, and prevail more than reasons drawn from worldly policy. 3. When we are so true to our aims and so fixed to our rule that no hopes or fears can sway us another way, but we are always looking to see what agrees with our rule or differs from it. 4. When we can do nothing against the truth, but only for the truth (2 Cor. 13:8), because it is dearer to us than our lives. Truth does not have this sovereignty in the heart of any carnal person. 5. When, if we were free to choose whose government we would live under, we would still, out of delight in the inner man in Christ’s government, choose Him alone to rule us before any other. For this shows that we are of one mind with Christ, a free and willing people, not forced into Christ’s service except by the sweet compulsion of love. When we are so pleased with the government of Christ’s Spirit that we are willing to surrender ourselves to Him in all things, then His kingdom has come into us, when our wills are brought to His will. It is the bent of our wills that makes us good or evil.

6. A well-ordered, consistent life, not lived in fits and starts, shows a well-ordered heart, just as in a clock, when the hammer strikes correctly and the hand on the dial points correctly, it is a sign that the wheels are rightly set. 7. When Christ’s will competes with some earthly loss or gain, and yet in that particular case the heart will bow to Christ, it is a true sign. For the truest test of the power of grace is in particular cases that touch us most closely, because there our corruption is strongest. When Christ came close to home with the young man in the gospel (Matt. 19:22), He lost a disciple. 8. When we can practise duties that please Christ, though they are contrary to the flesh and to the way of the world; and when we can overcome ourselves in the evil our nature is prone and much inclined to, which suits the mood of the times and which others lie enslaved under, such as desire for revenge, hatred of enemies, private aims and the like. Then it is clear that grace is above nature in us, heaven above earth, and that it will have the victory.

To make this clearer and to help us in testing ourselves, we must know that there are three degrees of victory: 1. when we resist, though we are beaten; 2. when grace gets the upper hand, though with a struggle; 3. when all corruption is perfectly overcome. Now even when we have strength only to resist, we may still know that Christ’s government in us will be victorious. For what is said of the devil is true of all our spiritual enemies: if we resist, they will in time flee from us (James 4:7). For He who is in us, who takes the side of His own grace, is stronger than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4). And if we may hope for victory from mere resistance, what may we not hope for when the Spirit has gained the upper hand?

fields.title: Means to Make Grace Victorious
fields.body_html:
NOW for the second point, that is, directions.

We must know that, though Christ has undertaken this victory, He achieves it by training us up to fight His battles. He overcomes in us by making us wise unto salvation (2 Tim. 3:15). And to the degree that we believe Christ will conquer, to that degree we will strive by His grace to conquer, for faith is an obedient and a wise grace. Christ makes us wise to ponder and weigh things, and then to rank and order them so that we may better choose what is best. Some rules to help us judge are these:

Judge things by whether they help or hinder the main thing; by whether they further or hinder our final account; by whether they make us more or less spiritual, and so bring us nearer to the fountain of goodness, God Himself; by whether they bring us peace or sorrow in the end; by whether they commend us more or less to God, and in what we shall most approve ourselves to Him. Also judge things now as we shall judge them later, when the soul is best able to judge, as when we are under some public disaster, or at the hour of death, when the soul gathers itself in from everything else to itself. Look back on past experience, and see what agrees best with it, and what was best in our worst times. If grace is best, or was best then, it is best now. And work at judging things as He judges who must judge us, and as holy people judge who are led by the Spirit; more particularly, as those judge who have nothing to gain from the matter in question. For outward things blind the eyes even of the wise. We see that the Roman party is most corrupt in those things where their honour, ease or profit is at stake, but in the doctrine of the Trinity, which does not touch these things, they are sound. But it is not enough for judgment to be right; it must also be ready and strong.

Where Christ establishes His government, He breathes into us a care to keep the judgment clear and fresh, for while the judgment stands straight and firm, the whole structure of the soul stays strong and unconquerable. True judgment in us advances Christ, and Christ will advance it. All sin comes either from false principles, or from ignorance, or from forgetfulness or unbelief of true ones. Through thoughtlessness and weak assent, Eve first lost her hold (Gen. 3). So it is good to store up true principles in our hearts and to refresh them often, so that by virtue of them our affections and actions may be more vigorous. When the judgment is fortified, evil finds no way in, and good things have a party within us to welcome them. While true, convincing light continues, we will not do the least evil of sin to escape the greatest evil of punishment. “Surely in vain the net is spread in the sight of any bird” (Prov. 1:17). While the soul is kept on high, there is little danger from snares below. We lose our high regard for things before we can be drawn into any sin.

And because knowledge and affection help each other, it is good to keep up our affections of love and delight by every sweet inducement and divine encouragement. For what the heart likes best, the mind studies most. Those who can bring their hearts to delight in Christ know most of His ways. Wisdom loves those who love her. Love is the best host to truth; and when truth, being so lovely, is not received in the love of it (2 Thess. 2:10), it leaves the heart and will stay no longer. A successful strategy has been to begin by drawing away the love, in order to corrupt the judgment, because as we love, so we tend to judge. So it is hard to be passionate and wise in earthly things. But in heavenly things, where the judgment has first been rightly informed, the more our affections grow, the better and clearer our judgments will be, because our affections, however strong, can never rise high enough to match the excellence of those things. We see in the martyrs that once the sweet teaching of Christ had won their hearts, it could not be driven out again by all the tortures that the ingenuity of cruelty could invent. If Christ has once taken possession of the affections, there is no dislodging Him. A fire in the heart overcomes all the fires outside.

3. Wisdom also teaches us where our weakness lies and where our enemy’s strength lies. This stirs up a watchful fear in us, by which we are kept safe. For out of this godly watchfulness we keep the provocations that are active and working away from what is passive and quick to catch in us, as we keep fire away from gunpowder. Those who want to stop the breeding of harmful creatures will prevent conception first, by keeping male and female apart. This watchfulness will be greatly helped by observing closely what has helped or hindered a gracious state of mind in us. And it will make us careful not to consult flesh and blood, in ourselves or others. How else can we think that Christ will lead us out to victory, when we take counsel from His enemies and ours?

4. Christ also makes us careful to use all the means by which fresh thoughts and affections may be stirred up and kept alive in us. Christ so honours the use of means, and the care He puts into us, that He credits both our preservation and our victory to our care in keeping ourselves. “He that is begotten of God keepeth himself” (1 John 5:18), not by himself, but by the Lord, depending on Him in the use of means. We are safe only as long as we are wise enough to put ourselves in the way of every good advantage, of company and the like. By leaving God’s paths we leave His government, and so lose our good state of mind, and soon find ourselves overgrown with the opposite disposition. When we draw near to Christ in His ordinances, He draws near to us (James 4:8).

5. Keep grace in use. It is not sleepy habits,

but grace in use that keeps us safe. While the soul is busy in some ordinary or sacred work, the corruptions within us are largely held down, Satan’s ways in are blocked, the Spirit has an open way to enlarge Himself in us, and the guard of angels is closest to us. This course often prevails more against our spiritual enemies than direct opposition. Christ’s honour is at stake in upholding those who are about His work.

Sixthly, in all these directions we must look up to Christ, the life-giving Spirit, and make our resolutions in His strength. Though we are urged to cleave to the Lord with purpose of heart (Acts 11:23), we must still pray with David, “Lord... keep this for ever in the imagination of the thoughts of the heart of thy people, and prepare their heart unto thee” (1 Chron. 29:18). Our hearts in themselves are very loose and unsettled: “Unite my heart to fear thy name” (Psalm 86:11). Otherwise, without Him, our best intentions will fall to the ground. It is a pleasing request, made out of love to God, to ask Him for a state of soul He can delight in. So in using all the means, we must send up our desires and complaints to heaven, to Him, for strength and help, and then we may be sure that He will bring forth judgment unto victory.

Lastly, it helps the state of the soul to know what condition it should be in, so that we may order our souls accordingly. We should always be fit for fellowship with God, heavenly-minded in earthly business, and willing to be taken away from it to redeem time for better things. We should be ready at all times to depart from here, and to live in a condition we would be content to die in. We should have hearts prepared for every good duty, open to every good opportunity, and shut against every temptation, keeping our watch and always ready armed. As far as we fall short of these things, so far we have just cause to be humbled, and yet to press on so that we may gain more ground on ourselves, and make these things more familiar and lovely to us. And when we find our souls sinking in any way, it is best to lift them up at once by some awakening meditations: on the presence of God; on the strict account we must give; on the infinite love of God in Christ and its fruits; on the excellence of a Christian’s calling; on the short and uncertain time of this life; on how little good all the things that steal away our hearts will do us before long; and on how it will be with us for ever afterwards, according as we spend this little time well or badly. The more we let such thoughts sink into our hearts, the more we shall rise toward the state of soul we shall enjoy in heaven. When we grow careless about keeping our souls, God restores our taste for good things by sharp trials. This is how David, Solomon, Samson and others were restored. It is much easier to keep than to recover.

“But in spite of my striving, I seem to be standing still.”

Grace, like the seed in the parable, grows we know not how. Yet at length, when God sees fit, we shall see that all our effort has not been in vain. The tree falls at the last stroke, but all the earlier strokes helped bring it down.

Sometimes victory is held back because some Achan has not been found out; or because we are not humble enough, as Israel had the worst of it against the Benjamites until they fasted and prayed (Judges 20:26); or because we betray our helps, do not stay on guard, and do not yield at once to the promptings of the Spirit, who always reminds us of the best things if we would pay attention. Our own consciences will tell us, if we let them speak, that some sinful indulgence of ourselves is the cause. The way to prevail in this case is, 1. to win the victory over the pride of our own nature by taking shame on ourselves in humble confession to God; then, 2. to overcome the unbelief of our hearts by yielding to the promise of pardon; and then, 3. trusting in Christ’s help, to set ourselves against the sins that have prevailed over us. Then, having prevailed over ourselves, we shall easily prevail over all our enemies, and conquer every condition we are brought into.

fields.title: Everyone Should Take Christ’s Side
fields.body_html:
IF Christ will have the victory, then the best course for nations and states is to kiss the Son (Ps. 2:12), to embrace Christ and His religion, to side with Christ and own His cause in the world. His side will prove the stronger side in the end. Happy are we if Christ honours us so far as to use our help to fight His battle against the mighty (Judges 5:23). True religion in a state is like the main pillar of a house, or the pole of a tent, that holds everything up. 2. So too for families: let Christ be the chief governor of the family. And 3. let every one of us be a house for Christ to live in familiarly and to rule. Where Christ is, all happiness must follow. If Christ goes, everything will go. Where Christ’s government in His ordinances and His Spirit is, all lesser government will prosper. Religion breathes life and grace into all other virtues; without it they are like a fine portrait with no head. Where Christ’s laws are written in the heart, all other good laws are best obeyed. No one despises man’s law except those who first despise Christ’s. Of all people, a man guided by Christ is the best; and of all creatures in the world, a man guided by his own will and passions is, next to the devil, the worst. The happiness of weaker things lies in being ruled by stronger ones. It is best for a blind man to be guided by one who can see; it is best for sheep and other helpless creatures to be guided by man; and it is happiest for man to be guided by Christ, because His government is so victorious that it frees us from the fear and danger of our greatest enemies, and leads us toward the greatest happiness our nature is capable of. This should make us rejoice when Christ reigns in us. When Solomon was crowned, the people shouted so that the earth rang. How much more should we rejoice in Christ our King!

And likewise for those whose souls are dear to us, our aim should be that Christ may reign in them too; that they may be baptized by Christ with fire (Matt. 3:11), and that these sparks may be kindled in them. People work to encourage the spirit and mettle, as they call it, of those they bring up, because they think they will need it in the many affairs and troubles of this life. Oh, but let us encourage the sparks of grace in them! For a natural spirit will fail in great troubles, but these sparks will make them conquerors over the greatest evils.

If Christ’s judgment is to be victorious, then the papal system, being an opposing structure set up by human ingenuity to maintain a stately idleness, must fall. And it has already fallen in the hearts of those on whom Christ has shone. It is a lie, and founded on a lie: on the supposedly infallible judgment of a man subject to sin and error. When what is taken for a principle of truth turns out to be a principle of error, the more one relies on it, the greater the danger.

fields.title: Christ’s Government Will Be Openly Victorious
fields.body_html:
IT is not only said that judgment will be victorious, but that Christ will bring it forth openly to victory. From this we observe that grace will become glory, and will be plain for all to see. Christ conquers now, and has His purposes, but in a way that is somewhat invisible: His enemies inside and outside us seem to have the upper hand. But He will bring forth judgment unto victory in the sight of all. The wicked, who now shut their eyes, will see it to their torment. It will not be in the power of clever people to see or not see as they please. Christ will have power over their hearts. As His wrath will seize their souls directly, against their wills, so He will have power over the eyes of their souls, to see and know what will increase their misery. Grief will be fastened to all their senses, and their senses to grief.

Then all the false gloss they put on things will be wiped off. People want to have the reputation of good and yet the sweetness of evil. Nothing is so heartily opposed by them as the truth that exposes them to themselves and to the eyes of others, their chief care being how to patch things up with the world and with their own consciences. But the time will come when they will be driven out of this fools’ paradise, and the more cunning their handling of things has been, the greater their shame will be. Christ, whom God has chosen to display the chief glory of His excellencies, is now veiled with regard to His body, the Church. But before long He will come to be glorified in His saints (2 Thess. 1:10), and will not lose the clear display of any of His attributes. He will declare to all the world what He is, when there will be no glory but that of Christ and His bride. Those who are like smoking flax now will then shine like the sun in the sky (Matt. 13:43), and their righteousness will break out like the noonday (Psalm 37:6). The image of God in Adam had a commanding majesty in it, so that all creatures revered him. How much more will the image of God in its perfection command respect from all! Even now a secret awe is put into the hearts of the greatest toward those in whom they see any grace shining. That is why Herod feared John the Baptist. But what will this be in their day of being brought forth, which is called the day of the revealing of the sons of God (Rom. 8:19)? There will be more glorious times when the kingdoms of this world become the kingdoms of the Lord Jesus Christ (Rev. 11:15), and He will reign for ever. Then judgment and truth will have their victory. Then Christ will plead His own cause. Truth will no longer be called heresy and schism, nor heresy Catholic doctrine. Wickedness will no longer go masked and disguised. Goodness will appear in its own brightness and shine in its own beams. Things will be what they are. Nothing is hidden that will not be laid open (Matt. 10:26). Iniquity will no longer be carried on as a mystery. Deep deceivers, who think they can hide their counsels from the Lord, will no longer walk unseen as if in the clouds. As Christ will not quench the least spark He has kindled, so He will put out the brightest blaze of fine appearances that are not from above.

If this were believed, people would think more of sincerity, which alone will give us boldness, and would not look for things to cover their shame. Confidence in such cover makes people more presumptuous now, and it will expose them to greater shame later.

If judgment is to be brought forth to victory, then those who have been ruled by their own deceitful hearts and by a spirit of error will be brought forth to disgrace. The God who has joined grace and truth with honour has joined sin and shame together in the end, and all the ingenuity and power of man will never be able to separate what God has joined. Truth and godliness may be trampled on for a time; but as the two witnesses rose again after they were killed and stood on their feet (Rev. 11:11), so whatever is of God will at length stand on its own foundation. There will be a resurrection not only of bodies but of reputations. Can we think that He who threw the angels out of heaven will let dust and worms’ food run a contrary course and get away with it for ever? No; as truly as Christ is King of kings and Lord of lords (Rev. 19:16), so surely He will dash in pieces like a potter’s vessel all those clods of earth that rise up against Him (Psalm 2:9). “Who hath hardened himself against him, and hath prospered?” (Job 9:4). No, without doubt the wrath of man will turn to Christ’s praise (Psalm 76:10). What was said of Pharaoh will be said of all headstrong enemies who would rather lose their souls than their wills: they are raised up only so that Christ may gain glory for Himself in their ruin.

Let us, then, take care not to follow the ways of those whose ends we shall tremble at. No more fearful judgment can fall on human nature than to be given up to a corrupt judgment of persons and things, because it comes under the woe pronounced on those who “call evil good, and good evil” (Isaiah 5:20).

How they will be loaded with curses one day, those who abuse the judgment of others by trickery and flattery, deceiving and being deceived! Then the complaint of our first mother Eve will be taken up, but to no purpose: “The serpent beguiled me” (Gen. 3:13). Satan in this person or that deceived me; sin deceived me; a foolish heart deceived me. It is one of the highest points of wisdom to consider on what grounds we risk our souls. Happy will they be who, by Christ’s light, have a right judgment of things and let that judgment prevail over their hearts.

The souls of most people are drowned in their senses and carried away by weak opinions, raised from common mistakes and the shadows of things. And Satan is ready to swell the imagination of outward good and outward evil, making them greater than they are and spiritual things smaller, showing them through distorting lenses. And so people, trusting in vanity, defeat themselves in their own imaginings. It is a woeful condition when both we and what we prize so highly vanish together, as surely they will, as surely as Christ’s judgment will come to victory. And to the degree that the vain heart of man has been swollen to imagine a greater good in the things of this world than is really there, to that degree the soul will be swollen to feel its misery more when it sees its error. This is the difference between a godly wise man and a deluded worldling: what the one now judges to be vain, the other will later feel to be vain, when it is too late. But this is the vanity of our nature: though we avoid above all things being deceived and mistaken in present things, in the greatest matters of all we are willingly ignorant and misled.

fields.title: Christ Alone Advances This Government
fields.body_html:
THE fifth conclusion is that this government is set up and advanced by Christ alone: He brings judgment to victory. We both fight and prevail in the power of His might (Eph. 6:10). We overcome by the Spirit obtained by the blood of the Lamb (Rev. 12:11).

It is He alone who teaches our hands to war and our fingers to fight (Psalm 144:1). Nature, as corrupted, favours its own existence, and will defend itself against Christ’s government. Nature, considered by itself, cannot raise itself above itself to spiritual actions of a higher order and nature. So the divine power of Christ is needed to carry us above all our own strength, especially in duties where we meet greater opposition. For there not only nature will fail us, but ordinary grace too, unless there is a stronger and fresh supply. When someone takes up a burden heavier than usual, unless there is more strength than weight, he will be crushed under it. In the same way, for every hard encounter there must be a fresh supply of strength. So it was with Peter (Matt. 26:69): when he was attacked by a stronger temptation, and was not held up and propped by a mightier hand, he fell badly, in spite of his earlier strength. And once we have fallen, in raising us up again it is Christ who must do the work: 1. by removing, 2. by weakening, or 3. by holding back the hindrances against us; and 4. by advancing the power of His grace in us further than we had it before we fell. So when we have fallen, and have been bruised by our falls, let us go at once to Christ to bind us up again.

Let us know, then, that it is dangerous to look to ourselves for what we must have from Christ. Since the fall, all our strength lies in Him, as Samson’s lay in his hair (Judges 16:17). We are only subordinate agents, moving as we are moved and working as we are first worked on; free only as far as we are set free; no wiser or stronger in anything we undertake than He makes us at the time. It is His Spirit who sets in motion, enlivens and applies the knowledge and strength we have; otherwise it fails and lies useless in us. We work when we work on a present strength. So dependent spirits are the wisest and most able. Nothing is stronger than humility, which goes out of itself, and nothing weaker than pride, which rests on its own foundation. This should be noted all the more because by nature we put on a kind of divinity, setting about actions in the strength of our own abilities. But Christ says, “Without me ye can do nothing” (John 15:5), to apostles who were in a state of grace. He does not say, “You can do a little,” but “nothing.” Left to ourselves, how easily we are overcome! How weak we are to resist! We are like reeds shaken by every wind. We tremble at the very sound and thought of poverty, disgrace, losses and the like. We give in at once. We have no control over our eyes, tongues, thoughts and affections, but let sin pass in and out. How soon we are overcome by evil, when we ought to overcome evil with good! How many good intentions get stuck at birth and have no strength to come out! All this shows how nothing we are without the Spirit of Christ. We see how weak the apostles themselves were until they were clothed with power from on high (Matt. 26:69). Peter was blasted by the words of a servant girl. But after the Spirit of Christ came on them, the more they suffered, the more they were encouraged to suffer; their comforts grew with their troubles. So in every encounter, and especially the difficult ones, let us lift up our hearts to Christ, who has Spirit enough for us all in all our needs, and say with good Jehoshaphat, “Neither know we what to do: but our eyes are upon thee” (2 Chron. 20:12). The battle we fight is Yours, and the strength we fight with must be Yours. If You do not go out with us, we are sure to be beaten. Satan knows that nothing can prevail against Christ, or against those who rely on His power. So his study is how to keep us in ourselves and in created things. But we must always keep this in mind: what is begun in self-confidence will end in shame.

Christ’s way of bringing forth judgment to victory is by letting us see that we must depend on Him. From this come those spiritual desertions in which He often leaves us to ourselves, both as to grace and as to comfort, so that we may know that the source of these lies outside ourselves. That is why God is most seen on the mount, that is, in extremities (Gen. 22:14). That is why we are saved by the grace of faith, which carries us out of ourselves to rely on another; and why faith works best alone, when it has the least outward support. That is why we often fail in lesser conflicts and stand firm in greater ones: because in lesser ones we rest more on ourselves, and in greater ones we flee to the rock of our salvation, which is higher than we are. And that is also why we are stronger after defeats: because hidden corruption, unnoticed before, is now uncovered, and so we are brought to make use of pardoning mercy and sustaining power. One main reason for this way of dealing with us is that we should know it is Christ who gives both the will and the deed, and does so freely, according to His own good pleasure. So we should work out our salvation with watchful fear and trembling (Phil. 2:12), in case by irreverent and presumptuous living we give Him cause to hold back His gracious influence and leave us to the darkness of our own hearts.

Those who are under Christ’s government have the spirit of revelation, by which they see and feel a divine power sweetly and strongly enabling them to keep faith when they feel the opposite, hope in a hopeless state, love to God under signs of His displeasure, and heavenly-mindedness in the midst of worldly business and attractions pulling the other way. They feel a power keeping their patience, and even joy, in the midst of reasons for mourning, and inward peace in the midst of attacks. How is it that when we have been assailed by temptation and surrounded by troubles we have stood firm, except by a secret strength holding us up? To make so little grace so victorious over so great a mass of corruption needs a spirit more than human. It is like keeping a fire alive in the sea, and a piece of heaven, as it were, even in hell. Here we know where to find this power, and to whom to give the praise for it. And it is our happiness that it is hidden so safely for us in Christ, in One so near to God and to us. Since the fall, God will not trust us with our own salvation. It is both purchased and kept for us by Christ, and we are kept for it through faith, which is worked by the power of God and lays hold of that same power. Saint Paul sets out this power gloriously (Eph. 1:19) as, 1. a great power; 2. an exceeding power; 3. a working and mighty power; 4. such a power as was at work in raising Christ from the dead. The grace that is only a persuasive offer, which we are free to receive or refuse, is not the grace that brings us to heaven. God’s people feel a powerful work of the Spirit, not only revealing to us our misery and our deliverance through Christ, but emptying us of ourselves, as those redeemed from ourselves, pouring new life into us, and afterwards strengthening us and reviving us when we droop and hang our wings, and never leaving us until the conquest is complete.

fields.title: Victory Is Not Won without Fighting
fields.body_html:
THE sixth conclusion is that this prevailing government will not come without fighting. There can be no victory where there is no battle. In Isaiah it is said, “He shall bring forth judgment unto truth” (Isaiah 42:3); here it is said, “till he send forth judgment unto victory.” The words “send forth” have a stronger sense in the original: to send forth with force. This shows that where His government is truly present, it will be opposed until He gets the upper hand. Nothing is so opposed as Christ and His government, both inside us and outside us. And inside us, it is opposed most at our first conversion. Though corruption does not prevail so far as to undo the powerful work of grace, there is not only a possibility of opposing, but a tendency to oppose; and not only a tendency, but an actual resisting of the working of Christ’s Spirit, and that in every action. Yet there is no resistance that prevails so far as to undo the work of grace; in the end, corruption gives way to grace.

It takes a great deal to bring Christ into the heart and set up a judgment seat for Him to judge there. An army of lusts mutinies against Him. The utmost strength of most people’s efforts and abilities goes into keeping Christ from ruling in the soul. The flesh is always working to keep its own rule, and so it runs down the credit of whatever crosses it, such as God’s blessed ordinances, and it prizes highly anything, however dead and empty, that gives room to the liberty of the flesh.

And no wonder the spiritual government of Christ is so opposed. 1. Because it is government, and that limits the course of the will and puts a bridle on its wanderings. Everything natural resists what opposes it. So the corrupt will works to throw down all laws, and counts it noble not to be overawed, and a sign of a low spirit to fear anyone, even God Himself, until unavoidable danger seizes people. And then those who feared least when out of danger fear most when in it, as we see in Belshazzar (Dan. 5:6).

2. It is spiritual government, and so the flesh can bear it even less. Christ’s government brings into obedience the very thoughts and desires, which are the most direct and free products of the soul. Even if a person behaved so properly that his whole life was free from outward offensive breaches, still with Christ to be carnally or worldly minded is death (Rom. 8:6). He looks on a worldly mind with greater loathing than on any single offence.

“But Christ’s Spirit is in those who are to some degree earthly minded.”

That is true, but not as one who permits and supports it; rather as one who opposes it, subdues it, and in the end conquers it. Carnal people would gladly bring Christ and the flesh together, and would be content to submit to Christ with some reservation. But Christ will be no underling to any low desire. So where we permit ourselves any sinful lust, it is a sign that the keys were never handed over to Christ to rule us.

3. Again, this judgment is opposed because it is judgment, and people do not like to be judged and condemned. Now Christ, in His truth, puts them on trial, passes sentence against them, and commits them to the final judgment of the great day. So they take it on themselves to judge the truth that must judge them, but truth will be too strong for them. Man has a day now, which Saint Paul calls man’s day (1 Cor. 4:3), in which he climbs onto his bench and seizes the right to judge Christ and His ways. But God has a day in which He will set everything straight, and His judgment will stand. And the saints will have their time, when they will sit in judgment on those who judge them now (1 Cor. 6:2). Meanwhile Christ will rule in the midst of His enemies, even in the midst of our hearts (Psalm 110:2). So it is no sign of a good condition to find everything quiet and nothing at odds. For can we think that corruption, which is the elder in us, and Satan, the strong man who holds many strongholds in us, will give up possession quietly? No; not even a thought of goodness is noticed by him without his joining with corruption to kill it at birth. And as Pharaoh’s cruelty was directed especially against the male children, so Satan’s malice is directed especially against the most godly and courageous resolutions.

This, then, we should always expect: wherever Christ comes, there will be opposition. When Christ was born, all Jerusalem was troubled. So when Christ is born in anyone, the soul is in an uproar, and all because the heart is unwilling to give itself up to Christ to rule it.

Wherever Christ comes, He causes division: 1. not only between a person and himself, but 2. between person and person, and 3. between church and church. Christ is no more the cause of this disturbance than medicine is the cause of the upset in a disordered body, where harmful humours are the real cause; for the aim of medicine is the peace of the humours. But Christ thinks it fit that the thoughts of people’s hearts should be revealed, and He is set for the fall as well as the rising again of many in Israel (Luke 2:34).

In this way the desperate madness of people is laid bare: they would rather be under the guidance of their own lusts, and so of Satan himself, to their endless destruction, than put their feet into Christ’s fetters and their necks under His yoke. Yet in fact Christ’s service is the only true freedom. His yoke is easy, and His burden is like the burden of wings to a bird, which makes her fly higher. Satan’s government is a bondage rather than a government, and Christ gives up to it those who throw off His own. For then He gives Satan and his agents power over them, since they will not receive the love of the truth (2 Thess. 2:10). “Take him, Jesuit; take him, Satan; blind him and bind him, and lead him to perdition.” Those who take the most liberty to sin are the most complete slaves, because they are the most willing slaves. In everything the will is either the best or the worst. The further people go on in a wilful course, the deeper they sink into rebellion; and the more they cross Christ by doing what they want, the more they will one day suffer what they do not want.

Meanwhile they are prisoners in their own souls, bound over in their consciences to the judgment after death of Him whose judgment they would have nothing to do with in their lives. And is it not fair that they should find Him a severe judge to condemn them, when they would not have Him as a gentle judge to rule them?

fields.title: Be Encouraged to Go On Cheerfully, Confident of Prevailing
fields.body_html:
TO conclude, and to apply in general to ourselves all that has been said: we see the embattled, yet sure and hopeful, condition of God’s people. The victory does not rest on us but on Christ, who has taken it on Himself not only to conquer for us but to conquer in us. The victory does not depend on our own strength to win it, nor on our enemies’ strength to defeat it. If it rested on us, we might rightly be afraid. But Christ will maintain His own government in us and take our side against our corruptions; they are His enemies as well as ours. So let us be strong in the Lord and in the power of His might (Eph. 6:10). Let us not look so much at who our enemies are as at who our judge and captain is; not at what they threaten but at what He promises. We have more for us than against us. What coward would not fight when he is sure of victory? No one here is overcome except the one who will not fight. So when any base faintness seizes us, let us lay the blame where it belongs.

Discouragement, springing from unbelief and from the bad report the spies brought on the good land, moved God to swear in His wrath that they should not enter His rest. Let us take care that a spirit of faint-heartedness, springing from apparent difficulty and from the disgrace thrown on God’s good ways, does not provoke God to keep us out of heaven. We see here what we may look for from heaven. O beloved, it is a comforting thing to think of Christ rightly, to know what love, mercy and strength are laid up for us in the heart of Christ. A good opinion of the physician, we say, is half the cure. Let us use this mercy and power of His every day in our daily battles: “Lord Jesus, You have promised not to quench the smoking flax and not to break the bruised reed. Nourish Your own grace in me; do not leave me to myself; the glory will be Yours.” Let us not let Satan disguise Christ to us, making Him seem other than He is to those who are His. Christ will not leave us until He has made us like Himself, all glorious within and without, and presented us blameless before His Father. What a comfort this is in our battles with our unruly hearts, that it will not always be like this! Let us strive a little while, and we shall be happy for ever. When we are troubled by our sins, let us think that Christ has this charge from His Father, that He shall not quench the smoking flax until He has subdued all things. This puts a shield into our hands to beat back all the fiery darts of Satan (Eph. 6:16). He will object, “You are a great sinner.” We may answer, “Christ is a strong Saviour.” He will object, “You have no faith, no love.” “Yes, a spark of faith and love.” “But Christ will not regard that.” “Yes, He will not quench the smoking flax.” “But this is so little and weak that it will vanish and come to nothing.” “No, Christ will nourish it until He has brought judgment to victory.” And this much we already have for our comfort: even when we first believed, we overcame God Himself, as it were, by believing the pardon of all our sins, in spite of the guilt of our own consciences and His absolute justice. Now, having prevailed with God, what will stand against us if we can learn to make use of our faith?

Oh, what confusion this is to Satan, that he should labour to blow out a poor spark and yet not be able to quench it; that a grain of mustard seed should be stronger than the gates of hell; that it should be able to remove mountains of opposition and temptation thrown up by Satan and our rebellious hearts between God and us! Abimelech could not bear that it should be said a woman had killed him (Judg. 9:54). It must be a torment to Satan that a weak child, a woman, or a frail old man should put him to flight by a spirit of faith.

Since there is such comfort where there is even a little true grace, that it will be so victorious, let us often examine what God has worked in us. Let us search out our good as well as our evil, and be more thankful to God for the smallest measure of grace than for anything outward. It will be of more use and comfort than all this world, which passes away and comes to nothing. Yes, let us be thankful for that promised and certain victory, which we may rely on without presumption, as Saint Paul does: “Thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 15:57). See a flame in a spark, a tree in a seed; see great things in small beginnings. Do not look so much at the beginning as at the completion, and so we shall be in some measure joyful in ourselves and thankful to Christ. Nor must we argue from the lack of a great measure of grace to the lack of any grace at all in us. For faith and grace do not stand on a single indivisible point, so that whoever lacks a certain measure has none at all. As there is a great distance between a spark and a flame, so there is a great breadth between the least measure of grace and the greatest. And the one who has the least measure is within the circle of God’s eternal favour. Though he is not a shining light, he is a smoking wick, which Christ’s tender care will not let Him quench. And let all that has been said draw those who are not yet in a state of grace to come under Christ’s sweet and victorious government. For though we shall meet much opposition, if we strive, He will help us; if we fail, He will nourish us; if we are guided by Him, we shall overcome; if we overcome, we are sure to be crowned. And as for the present state of the Church, we see how forlorn it is now; yet let us comfort ourselves that Christ’s cause will prevail. Christ will rule until He has made His enemies His footstool (Psalm 110:1), not only to trample on, but to help Him mount higher in glory. Babylon will fall, for strong is the Lord God who judges her (Rev. 18:8). Christ’s judgment, not only in His children but also against His enemies, will be victorious, for He is King of kings and Lord of lords (Rev. 19:16). God will not always let Antichrist and his supporters revel and swagger in the Church as they do.

If we look at the present state of the Church of Christ, it is like Daniel among the lions, like a lily among thorns, like a ship not only tossed but almost covered by the waves. It is so low that its enemies think they have buried Christ, as far as His gospel is concerned, in the grave, and they think they can keep Him there from rising. But as Christ rose in His own person, so He will roll away every stone and rise again in His Church. How little support the Church and the cause of Christ have today! How strong a conspiracy there is against it! The spirit of Antichrist is now lifted up and marches on furiously; things seem to hang by a small and invisible thread. But our comfort is that Christ lives and reigns, and stands on Mount Zion in defence of those who stand for Him (Rev. 14:1). And when states and kingdoms dash against one another, Christ will take care of His own children and His cause, since there is nothing else in the world He values much. At this very moment the deliverance of His Church and the ruin of His enemies are being worked out. We do not see things in motion until Christ has done His work, and then we shall see that the Lord reigns.

Christ and His Church, when they are at their lowest, are nearest to rising. His enemies, at their highest, are nearest to a downfall.

The Jews have not yet come in under Christ’s banner. But God, who has persuaded Japheth to come into the tents of Shem, will persuade Shem to come into the tents of Japheth (Gen. 9:27). The fullness of the Gentiles has not yet come in (Rom. 11:25). But Christ, who has been given the uttermost parts of the earth for His possession (Psalm 2:8), will gather all the sheep His Father has given Him into one fold, so that there may be one fold and one shepherd (John 10:16).

The faithful Jews rejoiced to think of the calling of the Gentiles; and why should we not rejoice to think of the calling of the Jews?

The course of the gospel has so far been like that of the sun, from east to west, and so in God’s time it may go still further west. No creature can hinder the course of the sun, or stop the influence of heaven, or prevent the wind from blowing, much less hinder the prevailing power of divine truth, until Christ has brought all things under one head. And then He will present them all to His Father: “These are the ones You gave Me; these are the ones who have taken Me for their Lord and King, who have suffered with Me. My will is that they be where I am, and reign with Me.” And then He will deliver up the kingdom to God, even the Father, and put down all other rule and all authority and power (1 Cor. 15:24).

Let us, then, bring our hearts to holy resolutions, and set ourselves for what is good and against what is evil, in ourselves or in others, according to our callings, with this encouragement: that Christ’s grace and power will go along with us. What would have become of that great work of the reformation of religion, in the latter spring of the gospel, if people had not been armed with unconquerable courage to stride over every obstacle, in this faith: that the cause was Christ’s, and that He would not fail His own cause? Luther honestly confessed that he often handled matters rashly and with a mixture of passion. But when he acknowledged it, God did not take advantage of his errors. Because the cause was God’s, and his aims were holy, to promote the truth, and because he was a mighty man in prayer and strong in faith, God kindled through him a fire that all the world will never be able to quench. As our faith is, so is our encouragement to every duty. So let us strengthen faith, so that it may strengthen all the other graces. This very belief, that faith will be victorious, is a means of making it so in fact. So believe that though it is often like smoking flax, it will still prevail. If it prevails with God Himself in trials, will it not prevail over every other opposition? Let us wait a while, and we shall see the salvation of the Lord (Exod. 14:13). May the Lord reveal Himself more and more to us in the face of His Son Jesus Christ, and magnify the power of His grace in nourishing these beginnings of grace in the midst of our corruptions. May He make holy to us the thought of our own weaknesses, to humble us, and the thought of His tender mercy, to encourage us. And may He persuade us that, since He has taken us into the covenant of grace, He will not cast us off for these corruptions, which grieve His Spirit and also make us vile in our own eyes. And because Satan labours to obscure the glory of His mercy and to hinder our comfort by discouragements, may the Lord add this to the rest of His mercies: that we may make the right use of this grace, and not lose any portion of the comfort laid up for us in Christ. And may He be pleased to let the prevailing power of His Spirit in us be evidence that grace has truly begun, and a pledge of final victory, at the time when He will be all in all, in all His people, for all eternity. Amen.
